Subscribe More forecasts: Atlanta 30 day forecast Greater Des Moines/ Crime & Emergencies Bird Flu Slams Sac County Turkey Flock, Reynolds Declares Iowa Disaster By Casey Santiago Published on October 29, 2026 Source: uma dantara / Unsplash Iowa's first commercial bird flu outbreak in nearly a year has landed in Sac County, where officials confirmed H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza in a turkey flock numbering in the tens of thousands of birds. The detection, announced Wednesday, immediately triggered a state disaster declaration and renewed warnings about biosecurity as fall bird migration ramps up across the region. State officials confirmed the case in a commercial turkey flock in Sac County on October 28, according to Iowa Agribusiness Radio Network. The flock's size is reported differently depending on the outlet: the The Des Moines Register put the number at approximately 44,000 birds, while the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship told Iowa Capital Dispatch the flock held approximately 44,400 birds. Either way, it marks Iowa's eighth confirmed HPAI detection of 2026 and its first in a commercial operation since December 2025. Gov. Kim Reynolds responded by authorizing a disaster proclamation for Sac County, effective immediately through November 27, according to the Office of Gov. Kim Reynolds. The proclamation allows state and department resources to be deployed more easily to help contain and monitor the outbreak, the state capital newsroom reported. Outbreak response typically requires dispatching the affected flock and disposing of the dead birds, the same report notes. A Quiet Year Interrupted Before Wednesday, Iowa had reported seven 2026 outbreaks in backyard, mixed-species or game-bird flocks, according to Iowa Capital Dispatch. There had been no commercial-scale case since late last year. The last large Iowa outbreak hit in January, when a Kossuth County hatchery with roughly 25,000 pheasants, quail and chukar partridges was struck, a case also documented by the same capital newsroom. Wild birds can carry H5N1 without showing symptoms, making them an easy vector into domestic flocks, the agribusiness radio network reports. With fall migration underway, officials say biosecurity has become especially important for Iowa producers trying to keep the virus away from their barns. Iowa's Outsized Toll Iowa has had more total birds affected by bird flu than any other state since the nationwide outbreak began, according to USDA APHIS data cited by the state newsroom. The Register puts that cumulative toll at 30.8 million chickens, turkeys and other birds lost in Iowa alone, part of a national total of 210.2 million birds lost to the virus according to USDA figures. The broader outbreak has been running since February 2022 and typically intensifies each spring and fall as wild birds migrate. Iowa is far from alone this fall. APHIS has confirmed HPAI in commercial poultry and gamebird operations across five other states — Illinois, South Dakota, North Dakota, Wisconsin and Kansas — according to WATTPoultry. That included a massive flock of 934,600 egg-laying hens in Clinton County, Illinois, confirmed October 19, and a flock of 60,600 commercial meat turkeys in Dickey County, North Dakota, confirmed two days later. South Dakota alone has logged 17 affected commercial flocks so far in 2026, while a Wisconsin turkey operation of 41,400 birds and a Kansas gamebird operation of 29,000 birds rounded out the week's confirmations. What Officials Are Telling Producers and Consumers Poultry producers who suspect their birds have the virus are urged to contact a veterinarian immediately and report suspected cases to the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship, according to the agribusiness radio network. Warning signs include sudden deaths, reduced egg production, lack of energy or appetite, respiratory problems, and swelling or discoloration around the head and legs. State officials have encouraged producers and backyard flock owners alike to keep strengthening their biosecurity measures. For consumers, officials stress that poultry and egg products remain safe to eat when properly handled and cooked to an internal temperature of 165 degrees Fahrenheit. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention continues to assess the risk to the general public as low, and the virus is not currently known to spread between humans, according to Iowa Capital Dispatch's earlier reporting on a separate Kossuth County case. The CDC's own guidance notes that when exposure to sick or dead animals cannot be avoided, protective equipment should be worn during direct or close contact with carcasses, feces, litter or other potentially contaminated materials. Conditions Utah Halted Active Monitoring of Mink Farm Workers While Bird Flu Genomes Show Mutation Also Seen in Spain Published Oct 28, 2026 10:55 PM EDT By Elena Vega MADS CLAUS RASMUSSEN/Ritzau Scanpix | AFP via Getty Images Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on WhatsApp Genetic sequencing of bird flu from a Utah mink farm found a mutation in every sample that is rarely seen in wild birds and also appeared in Spain's 2022 mink outbreak, according to a preliminary genomic report posted Oct. 22, as Nature World News reported. Utah officials have not culled the animals and have stopped actively monitoring farm workers. The findings arrive as Washington confirms its first H5N1 case tied to a dairy worker. Together, the two outbreaks show the virus moving through mammals in the West, and state responses that vary widely. The risk to the general public remains low, health officials say, and no person-to-person spread has been found in the United States. The concern centers on workers and their families, and on whether repeated spread in mammals gives the virus more chances to adapt. Developing Story Note: This report covers new developments involving H5N1 bird flu in Utah mink and Washington dairy cattle. Information may change as authorities, researchers or public health agencies release additional findings. Latest verified update checked Oct. 28, 2026; the most recent genome data cover samples collected Aug. 7. Mink Genomes and Utah's Hands-Off Response Researchers from the National Institutes of Health, Britain's Pirbright Institute and France's CNRS analyzed 10 virus genomes from C&T Fenn Farms, about an hour's drive south of Salt Lake City. The virus belongs to the B3.13 genotype that has circulated in U.S. dairy cattle since 2024, and its closest relatives were Texas cattle samples from late May. All 10 mink samples carried a change called PB1-K388R, which was not found in the cattle viruses. What the mutation does is poorly understood, and the report does not show it makes the virus more dangerous to people. The analysis points to a single introduction around early July that spread undetected for weeks. Utah agriculture officials placed a verbal hold on moving animals and materials off the farm but have no plans to cull. "There's just not a lot of options out there," State Veterinarian Amanda Price told ProPublica, which reported that Spain and Finland depopulated infected fur farms. The USDA said it has no species-specific authority or dedicated program to cull, vaccinate, or compensate mink owners. The state also stopped actively monitoring farm workers after agriculture officials complained that farmers were annoyed by it, ProPublica found. A respiratory disease epidemiologist with the state health department said monitoring would resume only if there was evidence of human-to-human transmission. Reporters saw a worker with a visibly red eye, a common bird flu symptom, who was not tested, and the farm owner attributed it to dust. Washington Dairy Case and the Wider Mammal Picture MedicalDaily previously reported that H5N1 has reached eight Yakima County dairy herds and infected a dairy worker with mild eye and respiratory symptoms. The CDC confirmed the virus as H5N1 in its weekly FluView report published Oct. 23, the first H5 case in Washington linked to a dairy worker. The report states that human-to-human transmission of H5 bird flu "has not been identified in the United States." Sequences from the Washington herds have not been released, so it is not yet known whether they carry the same genotype or mutations as Utah's mink. The CDC has counted 72 human H5 cases since February 2024, according to its bird flu situation summary, last updated Oct. 15, with cases reported among dairy and poultry workers. Mink worry scientists for a specific reason. They are highly susceptible to both bird flu and seasonal human flu, which creates a setting where the viruses could swap genes. With estimated flu hospitalization rates already at their highest mid-October level since the 2010-11 season, CDC guidance that workers exposed to animals get seasonal flu shots carries added weight. The global link is concrete. Spain's 2022 outbreak carried the same PB1 change, and Spain and Finland responded by culling. The report's authors point to large surveillance gaps, which make it harder to judge whether the virus is changing. Farm Families, Raw Milk and Reasonable Precautions People who work with dairy cattle, mink, poultry, or other sick animals face the highest risk. Eye redness, cough, sore throat, fever, or body aches after animal contact should prompt a call to a clinician, mentioning the exposure, and the CDC urges testing even for mild symptoms like a red eye. Prescription flu antivirals work best when started early, so exposed workers should not wait to see if symptoms pass. Workers who fear losing pay or immigration trouble may avoid testing, and local health departments can answer questions about testing and protective gear. Eye protection, masks, and gloves reduce exposure, and family members of farm workers can ask local health departments about testing if someone at home becomes sick. For most households, pasteurized milk and dairy remain safe. Raw milk can carry the virus and should be avoided, according to the CDC's bird flu prevention guidance, and pets should be kept away from raw pet food and sick or dead birds. Households with no farm contact face low risk. Key questions remain open. The researchers judged frozen feed an unlikely source, but how the virus reached the farm is still unknown. The report's authors said they knew of no testing of nearby farms or wildlife, and officials have not said whether any Utah worker was infected or whether the virus has changed since August. Developing Story Timeline Oct. 23, 2026: ProPublica reported that Utah stopped actively monitoring mink farm workers and has no plan to cull. A worker with a red eye was not tested. Oct. 23, 2026: The CDC's FluView confirmed the Washington dairy worker's virus as H5N1. Oct. 22, 2026: Researchers posted a preliminary report on 10 Utah mink genomes. All carried the PB1-K388R mutation also seen in Spain. Oct. 15, 2026: Yakima Health District announced the human case. The worker was isolating at home and was not severely ill. Aug. 17, 2026: The USDA confirmed H5N1 on the Utah mink farm, the first detection in U.S. farmed mink. Samples had been collected Aug. 7. The mutation was identified in samples collected in August 2026 and was also found in Spain's 2022 mink outbreak. The publication date of the report is October 29, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The event occurred in Utah, specifically at C&T Fenn Farms, located about an hour's drive south of Salt Lake City. The affected population includes mink farm workers and their families, as well as the mink population at the farm.
analysis.event: Genetic sequencing of bird flu from a Utah mink farm revealed a mutation in every sample that is also seen in Spain's 2022 mink outbreak. Utah officials halted active monitoring of farm workers due to complaints about annoyance, and the state has no plans to cull the mink population. This is a preliminary genomic report and does not confirm the mutation's impact on human health.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The mutation PB1-K388R was found in all 10 mink samples but not in the cattle viruses. The risk to the general public remains low, and no person-to-person spread has been found in the United States. The concern is focused on workers and their families, and whether repeated spread in mammals could lead to increased adaptation of the virus.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Utah agriculture officials placed a verbal hold on moving animals and materials off the farm but have no plans to cull. analysis.brief_en: On October 28, 2026, Utah halted active monitoring of mink farm workers after genetic sequencing of bird flu samples from C&T Fenn Farms revealed a mutation also seen in Spain's 2022 mink outbreak. The mutation, PB1-K388R, was identified in all 10 mink samples but not in cattle viruses. Utah officials have not planned to cull the mink population, citing a lack of species-specific authority. The state's decision to stop monitoring was based on complaints from farmers, and officials stated it would resume only if human-to-human transmission is confirmed. The findings are preliminary, and the report does not indicate the mutation increases danger to humans. This report highlights the varied state responses to H5N1 outbreaks and the ongoing uncertainty surrounding the virus's behavior in different host species.

news.content_title: Bird flu is raging on a mink farm. It could spark a human pandemic, experts say, but officials won’t act.
news.content: Aster, a mink rescued from a fur farm. Julie Leopo for ProPublica See all topics This story was originally published by ProPublica , a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up to receive their biggest stories as soon as they’re published. The strain of bird flu that’s ripped through American barns for the last four years has killed two people who caught it from sick animals. But as far as anyone can tell, humans can’t spread it. The virus has remained a true “bird” flu, tailored to attach to avian cells, not invade human throats and noses, where coughing and sneezing reliably spew droplets. Under the right conditions, however, that could change. A single mutation could give the bird flu a foothold in people and spark a pandemic that experts fear could be deadlier than COVID-19. For that to happen, this bird flu would likely need to find an intermediate host — an animal vulnerable to viruses that infect both birds and humans. These animals would be crowded together, each infection raising the odds that a new strain could arise through mutation. Then, for that strain to jump across species, it would have to have access to humans and time to spread among them undetected. That perfect petri dish exists right now, a ProPublica investigation found. For over two months, an outbreak of bird flu has raged uncontrolled on a Utah farm that raises thousands of mink for fur. Mink have lungs and airways that on a cellular level are remarkably similar to those of people; they have caught and spread other flus and infected some humans with COVID-19. Instead of trying to stop the outbreak and prevent it from spilling into humans, state and federal officials have done little except try to keep its existence quiet, our investigation shows. The failure to act amounts to a cascade of missteps flu experts called “irresponsible” and “puzzling.” One called it “playing with fire.” Utah agriculture officials learned in mid-August that mink were dying of bird flu on C&T Fenn Farms, about an hour’s drive south from Salt Lake City, according to communications released under the state’s public records law. C&T Fenn Farms, a mink fur farm west of Provo, Utah, on Sept. 25. Julie Leopo for ProPublica Had poultry been infected, the playbook would have been clear: The strain is so virulent that if a single chicken tests positive, the U.S. government requires farmers to kill the whole flock to protect other farms as well as public health. Poultry farmers are reimbursed for the loss. But there are no federal rules for how to deal with sick mink. Handling Utah’s response was state veterinarian Amanda Price, who sought help from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which takes the lead on bird flu outbreaks involving poultry and cows. USDA officials said they didn’t regulate mink or have a vaccine that was approved to give them. And though officials with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention spoke with Price’s health department counterparts who were less involved with the outbreak, they never talked to her, and she never reached out. The threat of spillover has been far from the minds of Utah officials, records and interviews show. Instead, front and center have been the interests of a business raising animals to skin for luxury pelts to ship overseas. “It has been devastating,” Price told ProPublica of the outbreak and its impact on the farm’s owner. “This is his life’s work that he’s seeing be destroyed. I really hope that you understand the humanity behind this situation.” Flu experts were unequivocal that the government should have ordered the farm to cull its mink, as other countries have done . But Utah never seriously considered it. A fur trade representative warned Price that doing so would kill the business and, ultimately, the industry. Farms spend decades breeding mink to develop unique genetic lineages. “There’s just not a lot of options out there other than kind of sitting and waiting and seeing what happens,” Price said, noting that USDA officials did not urge her to kill the mink or make her feel like bird flu in mink was any riskier than infections in other animals that have caught it, like ducks and cows. Flu experts found that response surprising. “Every other country that I’m aware of that has had H5N1 in fur farms, depopulation has happened pretty quickly,” said Tom Peacock, an avian influenza researcher at the Pirbright Institute. “The fact that the first instinct wasn’t just to depopulate and figure stuff out later is very concerning to me.” And all the while, officials didn’t monitor the mink workers for symptoms, as guidance from the CDC urges. Their exposure is significant: Mink sneeze. They escape. They attack. “The mink are fierce,” said a Spanish-speaking “minkero” who works on a nearby farm, showing the scars he got from the aggressive, solitary creatures. “You get scared because the fucking thing bites, and it claws at you.” Right now in Washington state, officials are working to track down the contacts of a symptomatic person exposed to dairy cattle infected with bird flu. The patient is isolating at home. Utah public health officials used to do similar, proactive monitoring. But they stopped after complaints from their colleagues in the agriculture department that farmers were annoyed by it. “Us doing active monitoring was making it so that farms didn’t want to work with them,” said Pamela Gomez Pinedo, a respiratory disease epidemiologist for Utah’s health department. As a result, public health workers had a “pretty difficult time” getting details from agriculture officials, she said. A mink farmworker, sometimes referred to as a “minkero” among the Spanish-speaking community, shows scars from mink bites and scratches in Payson, Utah. Workers typically wear long gloves to protect themselves but can still be bitten or scratched. Julie Leopo for ProPublica As part of a 2025 agreement , the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food agreed to share information about bird flu outbreaks on farms — so long as the health officials didn’t do anything to track workers’ health. “We will only do active monitoring in the case of evidence of human-to-human transmission,” Pinedo said in emails with a CDC epidemiologist. As the outbreak stretched to a month, CDC officials expressed concerns, asking how anyone would know if a worker had been infected if they weren’t getting tested. Price said the state’s policy not to monitor workers is meant to allow farmers to decide whether to contact the health department, rather than “forcing it on them.” “If we started seeing people actively dying from this, obviously that would change how we respond to this,” she said. A telltale sign of bird flu infection in humans is eye redness. It is present in over 90% of cases and is often the sole symptom a person displays. Last Saturday, a ProPublica reporter tracked down two people who worked at the Utah mink farm. One had a visibly red eye. The CDC explicitly urges testing for the symptom . After ProPublica reached out to the farm, its owner, Chad Fenn, contacted the Utah County Health Department about the red eye, which had cleared up by Monday, he told ProPublica. He said the worker got dust in his eye; the department didn’t recommend testing. “They’re not going to do anything,” Fenn said. “They said they don’t see that there’s a need.” He said the department recommended testing only if other symptoms, like a cough or sore throat, developed. A half dozen flu experts had no shortage of adjectives to describe their disbelief at the government decisions not to cull the mink or monitor and test the workers. “It’s amazing to me,” said Gail Hansen, a former Kansas state public health veterinarian and epidemiologist. “Utah doesn’t want to be the epicenter of the next human flu outbreak, right?” Most of the new viruses that have shaken humanity in the past century have spilled over from animals. Ebolas likely came from fruit bats; HIV, from chimpanzees. The leading theory for COVID-19 is that it jumped from bats to humans via an intermediate host mammal such as a raccoon dog. And all the modern flu pandemics have been bird flu viruses that mutated to spread in humans. ProPublica reported extensively on spillover in a 2023 series called “Roots of an Outbreak.” To prevent more deadly spillovers, experts worldwide urge governments to take a “ one health ” approach to viral threats, treating dangers to animals as dangers to humans. That’s not happening in Utah, experts said after reviewing ProPublica’s findings. Both the state and federal government are to blame. “There’s no leader of this ‘one health’ team to take charge,” said Erin Sorrell, a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. “That is going to allow the virus to continue to circulate, potentially adapt and potentially spill over into another host, whether it’s avian, mammalian or human.” This strain of bird flu, which began ripping through American poultry farms in early 2022, has proved adept at jumping to other species. It took hold in cows in 2024 and since then has run rampant through dairies . Yet federal guidance to prevent the spread into mink farms hasn’t considered cows a threat. Farmers are encouraged to keep wild birds from infiltrating their barns and avoid feeding them raw poultry. It has said nothing about feeding beef parts to mink, which farmers commonly do in summer months to encourage the animals to put on weight and grow. Dairy cows, which are not “depopulated” if exposed to bird flu, can still be slaughtered with the meat sold to farms and humans even though researchers have found the virus in the tissues of sick cows . USDA officials have insisted that beef for human consumption is free of bird flu , in part because the virus concentrates itself in sections of the cow people don’t usually eat. Fenn said that the mink are routinely fed raw organs of livestock, including cows. The genomic data from the samples of mink lungs and brains sent from Utah to a USDA lab shows that the mink were stricken with the same strain of the virus that has spread in dairy herds. Officials said they didn’t know whether contaminated beef was the way the mink got infected. Cows graze in a field in Utah Valley, Utah. Julie Leopo for ProPublica In mink, the dairy strain of bird flu may have found a much better host for mutating into a human flu, because mink airways have an abundance of the type of cell receptors in people’s throats and noses that are a common pathway for infection. A 2024 study of the dairy strain of the bird flu found that a single mutation could switch the virus from preferring the bird-type receptors to human-type receptors. And in studies using ferrets , a close relative of mink, the virus acquired mutations that let it attack human-type cell receptors. It’s not clear to scientists just how much of an evolutionary leap would be needed for this strain of bird flu to spread among humans, or whether mink are the host that would allow that leap to happen. How this ultimately plays out “really depends on what happens with the virus,” said Meghan Davis, an epidemiologist at Johns Hopkins University. “We might get lucky, and a response that is not robust may not have dire consequences,” she said. “But we may get unlucky.” There’s also a risk of something called “reassortment,” where another flu virus could infect the same cell as a bird flu virus and swap wide swaths of genetic code already adapted to humans. The strain of bird flu that’s ripped through American barns for the last four years has killed two people who caught it from sick animals. But as far as anyone can tell, humans can’t spread it. The virus has remained a true “bird” flu, tailored to attach to avian cells, not invade human throats and noses, where coughing and sneezing reliably spew droplets. Under the right conditions, however, that could change. A single mutation could give the bird flu a foothold in people and spark a pandemic that experts fear could be deadlier than COVID-19. For that to happen, this bird flu would likely need to find an intermediate host — an animal vulnerable to viruses that infect both birds and humans. These animals would be crowded together, each infection raising the odds that a new strain could arise through mutation. Then, for that strain to jump across species, it would have to have access to humans and time to spread among them undetected. That perfect petri dish exists right now, a ProPublica investigation found. For over two months, an outbreak of bird flu has raged uncontrolled on a Utah farm that raises thousands of mink for fur. Mink have lungs and airways that on a cellular level are remarkably similar to those of people; they have caught and spread other flus and infected some humans with COVID-19. The failure to act amounts to a cascade of missteps flu experts called “irresponsible” and “puzzling.” One called it “playing with fire.” Utah agriculture officials learned in mid-August that mink were dying of bird flu on C&T Fenn Farms, about an hour’s drive south from Salt Lake City, according to communications released under the state’s public records law. USDA officials said they didn’t regulate mink or have a vaccine that was approved to give them. They attack. “The mink are fierce,” said a Spanish-speaking “minkero” who works on a nearby farm, showing the scars he got from the aggressive, solitary creatures. “You get scared because the fucking thing bites, and it claws at you.” Right now in Washington state, officials are working to track down the contacts of a symptomatic person exposed to dairy cattle infected with bird flu. analysis.brief_en: A ProPublica investigation reveals an uncontrolled outbreak of bird flu on a mink farm in Utah, raising concerns about the potential for human-to-human transmission and a pandemic. The outbreak, which has lasted over two months, involves thousands of mink, whose lungs and airways are similar to humans, making them a potential intermediate host. news.title_zh: 禽流感正在水貂养殖场肆虐。专家称,这可能引发人类大流行,但官员们不会采取行动。
news.source_body_en: A ProPublica investigation reveals an uncontrolled outbreak of bird flu on a mink farm in Utah, raising concerns about the potential for human-to-human transmission and a pandemic. The outbreak, which has lasted over two months, involves thousands of mink, whose lungs and airways are similar to humans, making them a potential intermediate host. Despite the risk, state and federal officials have taken little action, prioritizing the fur trade interests over public health. Two people have died from bird flu contracted from infected mink, but no human-to-human spread has been confirmed. Experts warn that a single mutation could allow the virus to infect humans more easily, but officials have not implemented monitoring or culling measures. The CDC urges testing for symptoms like eye redness, which is a common sign of infection, but Utah health officials have not acted on this guidance. The lack of federal oversight and the failure to monitor workers have been criticized as "irresponsible" and "puzzling" by flu experts.

READ SUMMARY SUBSCRIBE RECEIVE IN PAPER OTHER EDITIONS Back Animal Health & Pathology 29 Oct 2026 H5N1 Pathology Reveals Species-Specific Patterns of Organ Damage in Poultry Highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) can produce different patterns of organ damage across poultry species. Understanding these differences is essential [...] Sahar Darazi SAVE IN THE LIBRARY PDF FILE Highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) can produce different patterns of organ damage across poultry species. Understanding these differences is essential for improving disease diagnosis, pathological investigations, and surveillance. POULTRY HEALTH & PATHOLOGY A Global Poultry-Health Challenge Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI), particularly the H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b lineage, remains a major concern for poultry production and animal health worldwide. Beyond its rapid spread and potential to cause substantial mortality, understanding how the virus damages different organs is essential for improving disease diagnosis and surveillance. A 2026 study published in Poultry Science investigated naturally occurring H5N1 infections in poultry in Taiwan, examining pathological changes across multiple species. The findings provide insights into how the same viral lineage can produce different disease patterns depending on the host species (1). KEY SCIENTIFIC FINDING Continue after advertising. The same H5N1 viral lineage can produce different patterns of organ damage and cellular responses across poultry species. Different Species, Different Pathological Responses Researchers examined samples from 41 H5N1-positive farms, including 23 chicken farms, four duck farms, ten goose farms, and four quail farms. The investigation combined gross pathology, histopathology, immunohistochemistry, and analyses of cellular apoptosis. The researchers evaluated tissues from several organs, including the brain, heart, liver, spleen, lungs, kidneys, and pancreas. CHICKENS Widespread systemic infection, extensive tissue necrosis, and viral antigen distribution. DUCKS Generally milder lesions and a more coordinated apoptotic response. GEESE Intermediate pathological characteristics. QUAILS A distinct pattern involving prominent splenic lesions and different relationships between viral distribution, cell death, and tissue damage. These differences demonstrate why clinical signs or examination of a single organ may not fully characterize the severity and distribution of HPAI infection (1). Why Diagnostic Pathology Matters Gross examination can identify visible abnormalities, including haemorrhages, organ enlargement, and tissue discoloration. However, these findings may overlap with those associated with other infectious diseases. Histopathology allows veterinarians to examine tissue architecture and cellular injury under a microscope. Immunohistochemistry helps identify viral antigens within affected tissues, allowing investigators to assess viral distribution. The study also investigated apoptosis, the regulated process of cell death. Comparing apoptotic signals with tissue lesions and viral antigen distribution helps clarify how infection and host responses contribute to organ damage. A review of avian diagnostic pathology emphasizes the potential value of combining conventional pathological examination with molecular diagnostics, immunohistochemistry, and digital pathology. Artificial intelligence and machine learning may further support diagnostic interpretation and disease surveillance as these technologies develop (2). Implications for Poultry Disease Surveillance Pathological severity and viral distribution are not necessarily identical across poultry species. Diagnostic investigations should consider the host species, clinical history, affected organs, and laboratory findings rather than relying on one visible lesion or symptom. For poultry veterinarians and diagnostic laboratories, a structured investigation combining necropsy, tissue examination, and confirmatory laboratory testing can support more accurate characterization of suspected outbreaks. These findings do not establish a universal pathological pattern for every H5N1 infection. The study was based on naturally infected farms in Taiwan, and its results should be interpreted within that epidemiological context. Nevertheless, the research strengthens the case for integrating species-specific pathology with laboratory confirmation and surveillance to improve understanding of HPAI and other emerging poultry diseases. Scientific References (1) Yi, Z.-J., Huang, Y.-I., Lin, Y.-J., Tsai, Y.-W., Cheng, M.-C., & Chen, Y.-M. (2026). Comprehensive pathological, immunohistochemical, and apoptotic analysis of the highly pathogenic avian influenza A virus H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b in poultry in Taiwan. Poultry Science. Read the scientific study → (2) Getnet, G. M., Getnet, M. A., & Atenaf, A. S. (2026). Advances in Avian Diagnostic Pathology: Current Trends, Challenges and Future Directions: A Review. Veterinary Medicine and Science, 12(3), e70905. analysis.brief_en: A 2026 study published in Poultry Science investigated naturally occurring H5N1 infections in poultry in Taiwan, examining pathological changes across multiple species. The research, conducted on 41 H5N1-positive farms (23 chicken, 4 duck, 10 goose, 4 quail), revealed species-specific patterns of organ damage and cellular responses. These differences underscore the limitations of relying on a single visible lesion or symptom for diagnosing HPAI infections. news.title_zh: H5N1 病理学揭示家禽器官损伤的物种特异性模式 - aviNews
news.source_body_en: A 2026 study published in Poultry Science investigated naturally occurring H5N1 infections in poultry in Taiwan, examining pathological changes across multiple species. The research, conducted on 41 H5N1-positive farms (23 chicken, 4 duck, 10 goose, 4 quail), revealed species-specific patterns of organ damage and cellular responses. These differences underscore the limitations of relying on a single visible lesion or symptom for diagnosing HPAI infections. The study combined gross pathology, histopathology, immunohistochemistry, and apoptosis analysis to better understand the disease's impact. It highlights the need for a structured investigation that considers host species, clinical history, affected organs, and laboratory findings. The findings do not establish a universal pattern for all H5N1 infections but reinforce the value of integrating species-specific pathology with surveillance and diagnostics. The research also suggests that future advancements in diagnostic technologies, such as artificial intelligence, could enhance disease monitoring and interpretation.
news.content_zh: 2026 年《家禽科学》上发表的一项研究调查了台湾家禽中自然发生的 H5N1 感染,检查了多个物种的病理变化。这项研究在 41 个 H5N1 阳性农场(23 个鸡、4 个鸭、10 个鹅、4 个鹌鹑)中进行,揭示了器官损伤和细胞反应的物种特异性模式。这些差异强调了依靠单一可见病变或症状来诊断 HPAI 感染的局限性。该研究结合了大体病理学、组织病理学、免疫组织化学和细胞凋亡分析,以更好地了解该疾病的影响。它强调需要进行结构化调查,考虑 宿主 物种、临床病史、受影响的器官和实验室检查结果。研究结果并未建立所有 H5N1 感染的通用模式,但强化了将物种特异性病理学与 监测 和诊断相结合的价值。该研究还表明,人工智能等诊断技术的未来进步可以增强疾病监测和解释。

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Universal influenza vaccine platforms advance toward broader H5N1 pandemic readiness by October 28, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 7 mins read 0 Universal influenza vaccine platforms advance toward broader H5N1 pandemic readiness Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A newly published review in Discover Immunity examines how universal influenza vaccine platforms could strengthen the world’s defenses against H5N1 avian influenza, a virus the authors describe as a significant threat to global public health. The review, published on 4 October 2026 as an open-access article, brings together current evidence on licensed and experimental H5N1 vaccines, the immunological factors that shape their performance, and the manufacturing and distribution systems that would determine whether an effective response to an outbreak is even possible. Its central argument is that protection against a virus as antigenically variable as H5N1 cannot rest on strain-matched vaccines alone, but requires platforms built around conserved regions of the virus that can generate durable, cross-protective immunity against multiple variants. The review begins by situating H5N1 within the broader landscape of zoonotic threats. H5N1 avian influenza is described as a particularly dangerous strain of influenza A virus because it can infect both birds and humans. First identified in Hong Kong in 1997, the virus has since caused periodic outbreaks in poultry and wild birds across global regions, with occasional human infections that have had fatal consequences. Highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses kill large quantities of poultry and impose significant economic losses on the poultry industry worldwide. In humans, the review notes, H5N1 infection can lead to acute respiratory distress and organ failure, with a fatality rate described as extremely high compared with seasonal influenza strains. Human infections occur mainly through close contact with infected chickens or contaminated environments, and the possibility that mutations could enable sustained human-to-human transmission remains a central concern. The virus’s rapid mutation rate and its potential for human-to-human spread are cited as the reasons it has become a priority for global health surveillance and preparedness. Against this background, the review assesses what current H5N1 vaccine platforms actually deliver. Licensed, prepandemic and stockpiled H5N1 vaccines are inactivated and recombinant hemagglutinin vaccines, developed with or without adjuvants. The immunogenicity literature indicates that adjuvanted preparations consistently induce higher hemagglutination inhibition and neutralizing antibody titers than non-adjuvanted preparations, and reach seroprotective titers, defined as an HAI titer of at least 1:40, with lower antigen doses and fewer injections. Oil-in-water adjuvants such as AS03 and MF59 stimulate B cell responses to antigens and engage T follicular helper cells, increasing the extent and persistence of humoral immune responses. Strain-specific neutralization is strong with inactivated adjuvanted vaccines when the vaccine matches the circulating H5N1 clade, but cross-reactivity against heterologous clades is inconsistent and mostly inferior. Recombinant hemagglutinin vaccines containing conserved stalk epitopes show slight enhancement of cross-clade responses, yet neutralizing titers against divergent H5N1 subclades often fall below presumptive protective thresholds without booster immunizations. Discover more vaccine Find Vaccines vaccines Get Cold Relief Read Med Journals A crucial limitation the review emphasizes is the near-total absence of real-world effectiveness data. Because there has been no sustained human-to-human transmission of H5N1, H5N1 vaccines have generated few field effectiveness data, and licensure and stockpiling decisions have instead relied on surrogate endpoints, namely immunogenicity correlates such as HAI and neutralization titers. Pre-licensure clinical experience in high-risk groups such as poultry workers shows acceptable safety and immunogenicity, but conclusive protective effectiveness against natural H5N1 infection has not been determined. The authors conclude that although these vaccines achieve high immunogenicity against homologous strains when boosted with adjuvant, their heterologous breadth is poor, and no real-world effectiveness data currently exist to support vaccine optimization and real-time assessment during an actual outbreak. The review then turns to next-generation candidates designed for safety, immunogenicity and cross-protection. It describes H5N1 as now an established, year-round infection whose host range has expanded to include many mammals. The virus’s pathogenicity is attributed mainly to the acquisition of a polybasic hemagglutinin cleavage site, which facilitates systemic spread, alongside emerging endothelial and neurotropic properties that produce severe disease and high mortality in mammals. H5N1 has been observed to accumulate mutations linked to mammalian adaptation, albeit with limited transmission, notably in the hemagglutinin and polymerase complex. Novel mammalian reservoirs, including dairy cattle in the United States, raise human exposure risk. In response, vaccine development is shifting from older adjuvanted inactivated vaccines toward new platforms, with mRNA and virus-like particle vaccines being developed for rapid rollout and broader immune responses. The review highlights the speed of mRNA production, achievable in weeks from sequence reads, as making it one of the most promising pandemic platforms. Discover more Study Biology Track Outbreaks Biology textbook sales Several experimental strategies receive detailed attention. Live attenuated influenza virus vaccines based on NS segment truncation prevent influenza virus infection and have shown promise as vaccine candidates among other platforms, though the authors argue that more attention must turn to LAIV development platforms to produce a truly universal influenza vaccine candidate. H5 antigens expressed by recombinant adenovirus and vesicular stomatitis virus vectors induce robust humoral and cellular immunity in individuals after single vaccinations; non-replicating adenoviral vectors have proven safe, while replicating VSV platforms can activate stronger innate responses. Pre-existing anti-vector immunity is a recognized consideration, which heterologous prime-boost regimens can alleviate. Structure-guided design uses computational algorithms to stabilize hemagglutinin in its pre-fusion conformation or to display conserved epitopes, and computationally optimized broadly reactive antigens, known as COBRAs, extend cross-clade neutralization by concentrating on conserved regions. These antigens can be deployed across delivery systems including mRNA and protein formats. Universal strategies targeting the conserved hemagglutinin stem, the matrix protein 2 ectodomain, or internal proteins such as NP and M1 aim to induce cross-subtype protection, while chimeric hemagglutinin constructs, mosaic nanoparticles and multi-epitope chimeras are designed to address the antigenic diversity of H5 lineages. Despite these efforts, the review notes a persistent lack of broadly reactive antibody induction capable of conferring broad, long-lasting protection. The review also examines what determines whether an H5N1 vaccine works in a given person or population. AS03-adjuvanted H5N1 vaccine generates substantially more potent immune responses than non-adjuvanted vaccine, and one study found the adjuvant may boost responses by switching off the NR4A1 and SDC1 genes, switching on the ID3 gene and decreasing cortisol production, although the mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Two-dose schedules with a three-week interval have induced high neutralizing antibody levels against the vaccine strain, and protection may persist for up to three years after two doses of AS03-adjuvanted H5N1 vaccines, with the prime-boost schedule producing robust anamnestic antibody responses that are cross-protective. However, prior antigenic imprinting, or original antigenic sin, can shape future responses: B cell repertoires focus on conserved epitopes from initial exposure, which may suppress responses to new antigenic variants and limit the breadth of neutralizing responses, potentially reducing seroconversion to drifted antigens. Host genetics also matter, as single-nucleotide polymorphisms in pattern recognition receptors such as TLR7 and TLR8 and in cytokine regulators determine the magnitude of antibody and T cell responses. Immunosenescence reduces both humoral and cellular responses, with most older adults showing reduced HAI titers after vaccination, and comorbidities such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease and immunosuppression further lower responsiveness. On the viral side, antigenic drift in hemagglutinin and neuraminidase can produce circulating strains that no longer match vaccine antigens, reassortment can generate combinations against which pre-existing immunity offers minimal protection, and suboptimal poultry vaccination coverage can select drifted variants in reservoirs, complicating human vaccine strain selection and raising zoonotic spillover risk. Adjuvants emerge as a key lever for improving and shaping immunity. Oil-in-water adjuvants such as AS03 and MF59 enable reduced antigen doses while achieving high seroconversion by improving antigen uptake by antigen-presenting cells and triggering strong innate signaling, a dose-sparing capability the review considers especially valuable when pandemic production capacity is limited. Adjuvants activate diverse B cell clones and drive antibody affinity maturation, which may expand cross-clade neutralization breadth against antigenically drifted H5N1 strains, an important property for prepandemic stockpiles where the future strain cannot be predicted. Newer adjuvant preparations containing toll-like receptor agonists and synthetic immunomodulators are engineered to favor balanced Th1 and Th2 responses. In older adults and immunocompromised individuals, who commonly respond poorly to unadjuvanted vaccines, higher doses of adjuvants that strongly activate innate immunity, such as TLR4 agonists and saponin formulations, can partially address these limitations by enhancing dendritic cell activation and cytokine milieus. The review cautions that reactogenicity, including local pain and temporary systemic responses, must be assessed, and that while AS03 and MF59 have shown generally acceptable safety in controlled studies, continued surveillance across different populations is crucial. On evaluation methods, the review describes a tiered pathway. Preclinical tests in mice, ferrets and non-human primates establish safety, immunogenicity and protective effect, with ferrets considered the best influenza model because their respiratory anatomy and disease progression resemble those of humans. Hemagglutination inhibition titers remain a key correlate of protection, neutralization tests measure the strength of serum antibodies against viral entry, and cellular immunity assays such as ELISpot and intracellular cytokine staining quantify T cell responses associated with viral clearance and cross-clade coverage. Robust correlates accelerate development by reducing reliance on large efficacy trials that are ethically or logistically infeasible in prepandemic phases. Phase III randomized controlled trials in target populations typically use laboratory-confirmed influenza illness as the endpoint, and after approval, observational studies including cohort, case-control and test-negative designs assess real-world performance against circulating strains. Recent work illustrates the pipeline: an mRNA vaccine expressing the hemagglutinin of the first bovine-to-human strain, A/Texas/37/2024, stimulated strong, long-lasting humoral responses and a balanced Th1/Th2 profile in murine studies, providing 100 percent protection against lethal homologous challenge, and produced cross-clade binding antibody responses with a favorable safety profile in rats. Separately, an H5N1 vaccine cultured in serum-free MDCK cell suspension protected mice in challenge tests, with antibodies persisting up to eight months after the first dose in rats and elevated IP-10 levels indicating enhanced innate immunity. The review closes by linking vaccine science to delivery and equity. Intradermal delivery targets the immune cells of the skin and can achieve strong responses with lower antigen doses, extending scarce vaccine supplies, though it requires specialized equipment and trained personnel. Microneedle patches offer needle-free, self-administered vaccination with thermostability that removes cold-chain constraints, although mass production and regulatory licensing remain hurdles. Mucosal intranasal vaccines induce both systemic and mucosal immunity at the respiratory entry point but face stability and formulation issues. Heterologous prime-boost regimens, such as intramuscular priming followed by mucosal boosting, may make immunity more durable and broader against variants. The authors argue that equitable global distribution frameworks such as COVAX must ensure vaccines reach low- and middle-income countries based on need, with high-risk groups prioritized. Combined, they conclude, universal vaccines targeting conserved regions, durable cross-protection, agile manufacturing and fair distribution form the strategy they identify as most capable of reducing the threat of an H5N1 pandemic and improving global preparedness. S., Kamal, M. A., & Nazari, M. J. (2026). Recent advances in universal influenza vaccine platforms: paving the way for universal H5N1 vaccines and pandemic readiness. The immunogenicity literature indicates that adjuvanted preparations consistently induce higher hemagglutination inhibition and neutralizing antibody titers than non-adjuvanted preparations, and reach seroprotective titers, defined as an HAI titer of at least 1:40, with lower antigen doses and fewer injections. Oil-in-water adjuvants such as AS03 and MF59 stimulate B cell responses to antigens and engage T follicular helper cells, increasing the extent and persistence of humoral immune responses. Strain-specific neutralization is strong with inactivated adjuvanted vaccines when the vaccine matches the circulating H5N1 clade, but cross-reactivity against heterologous clades is inconsistent and mostly inferior. Recombinant hemagglutinin vaccines containing conserved stalk epitopes show slight enhancement of cross-clade responses, yet neutralizing titers against divergent H5N1 subclades often fall below presumptive protective thresholds without booster immunizations. Discover more vaccine Find Vaccines vaccines Get Cold Relief Read Med Journals A crucial limitation the review emphasizes is the near-total absence of real-world effectiveness data. Because there has been no sustained human-to-human transmission of H5N1, H5N1 vaccines have generated few field effectiveness data, and licensure and stockpiling decisions have instead relied on surrogate endpoints, namely immunogenicity correlates such as HAI and neutralization titers. Pre-licensure clinical experience in high-risk groups such as poultry workers shows acceptable safety and immunogenicity, but conclusive protective effectiveness against natural H5N1 infection has not been determined. The authors conclude that although these vaccines achieve high immunogenicity against homologous strains when boosted with adjuvant, their heterologous breadth is poor, and no real-world effectiveness data currently exist to support vaccine optimization and real-time assessment during an actual outbreak. The review then turns to next-generation candidates designed for safety, immunogenicity and cross-protection. It describes H5N1 as now an established, year-round infection whose host range has expanded to include many mammals. The virus’s pathogenicity is attributed mainly to the acquisition of a polybasic hemagglutinin cleavage site, which facilitates systemic spread, alongside emerging endothelial and neurotropic properties that produce severe disease and high mortality in mammals. H5N1 has been observed to accumulate mutations linked to mammalian adaptation, albeit with limited transmission, notably in the hemagglutinin and polymerase complex. Novel mammalian reservoirs, including dairy cattle in the United States, raise human exposure risk. In response, vaccine development is shifting from older adjuvanted inactivated vaccines toward new platforms, with mRNA and virus-like particle vaccines being developed for rapid rollout and broader immune responses. The review highlights the speed of mRNA production, achievable in weeks from sequence reads, as making it one of the most promising pandemic platforms. Discover more Study Biology Track Outbreaks Biology textbook sales Several experimental strategies receive detailed attention. Live attenuated influenza virus vaccines based on NS segment truncation prevent influenza virus infection and have shown promise as vaccine candidates among other platforms, though the authors argue that more attention must turn to LAIV development platforms to produce a truly universal influenza vaccine candidate. H5 antigens expressed by recombinant adenovirus and vesicular stomatitis virus vectors induce robust humoral and cellular immunity in individuals after single vaccinations; non-replicating adenoviral vectors have proven safe, while replicating VSV platforms can activate stronger innate responses. Pre-existing anti-vector immunity is a recognized consideration, which heterologous prime-boost regimens can alleviate. Structure-guided design uses computational algorithms to stabilize hemagglutinin in its pre-fusion conformation or to display conserved epitopes, and computationally optimized broadly reactive antigens, known as COBRAs, extend cross-clade neutralization by concentrating on conserved regions. These antigens can be deployed across delivery systems including mRNA and protein formats. Universal strategies targeting the conserved hemagglutinin stem, the matrix protein 2 ectodomain, or internal proteins such as NP and M1 aim to induce cross-subtype protection, while chimeric hemagglutinin constructs, mosaic nanoparticles and multi-epitope chimeras are designed to address the antigenic diversity of H5 lineages. Despite these efforts, the review notes a persistent lack of broadly reactive antibody induction capable of conferring broad, long-lasting protection. The review also examines what determines whether an H5N1 vaccine works in a given person or population. AS03-adjuvanted H5N1 vaccine generates substantially more potent immune responses than non-adjuvanted vaccine, and one study found the adjuvant may boost responses by switching off the NR4A1 and SDC1 genes, switching on the ID3 gene and decreasing cortisol production, although the mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Two-dose schedules with a three-week interval have induced high neutralizing antibody levels against the vaccine strain, and protection may persist for up to three years after two doses of AS03-adjuvanted H5N1 vaccines, with the prime-boost schedule producing robust anamnestic antibody responses that are cross-protective. However, prior antigenic imprinting, or original antigenic sin, can shape future responses: B cell repertoires focus on conserved epitopes from initial exposure, which may suppress responses to new antigenic variants and limit the breadth of neutralizing responses, potentially reducing seroconversion to drifted antigens. Host genetics also matter, as single-nucleotide polymorphisms in pattern recognition receptors such as TLR7 and TLR8 and in cytokine regulators determine the magnitude of antibody and T cell responses. Immunosenescence reduces both humoral and cellular responses, with most older adults showing reduced HAI titers after vaccination, and comorbidities such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease and immunosuppression further lower responsiveness. On the viral side, antigenic drift in hemagglutinin and neuraminidase can produce circulating strains that no longer match vaccine antigens, reassortment can generate combinations against which pre-existing immunity offers minimal protection, and suboptimal poultry vaccination coverage can select drifted variants in reservoirs, complicating human vaccine strain selection and raising zoonotic spillover risk. Adjuvants emerge as a key lever for improving and shaping immunity. Oil-in-water adjuvants such as AS03 and MF59 enable reduced antigen doses while achieving high seroconversion by improving antigen uptake by antigen-presenting cells and triggering strong innate signaling, a dose-sparing capability the review considers especially valuable when pandemic production capacity is limited. Adjuvants activate diverse B cell clones and drive antibody affinity maturation, which may expand cross-clade neutralization breadth against antigenically drifted H5N1 strains, an important property for prepandemic stockpiles where the future strain cannot be predicted. Newer adjuvant preparations containing toll-like receptor agonists and synthetic immunomodulators are engineered to favor balanced Th1 and Th2 responses. In older adults and immunocompromised individuals, who commonly respond poorly to unadjuvanted vaccines, higher doses of adjuvants that strongly activate innate immunity, such as TLR4 agonists and saponin formulations, can partially address these limitations by enhancing dendritic cell activation and cytokine milieus. The review cautions that reactogenicity, including local pain and temporary systemic responses, must be assessed, and that while AS03 and MF59 have shown generally acceptable safety in controlled studies, continued surveillance across different populations is crucial. On evaluation methods, the review describes a tiered pathway. Preclinical tests in mice, ferrets and non-human primates establish safety, immunogenicity and protective effect, with ferrets considered the best influenza model because their respiratory anatomy and disease progression resemble those of humans. Hemagglutination inhibition titers remain a key correlate of protection, neutralization tests measure the strength of serum antibodies against viral entry, and cellular immunity assays such as ELISpot and intracellular cytokine staining quantify T cell responses associated with viral clearance and cross-clade coverage. Robust correlates accelerate development by reducing reliance on large efficacy trials that are ethically or logistically infeasible in prepandemic phases. Phase III randomized controlled trials in target populations typically use laboratory-confirmed influenza illness as the endpoint, and after approval, observational studies including cohort, case-control and test-negative designs assess real-world performance against circulating strains. Recent work illustrates the pipeline: an mRNA vaccine expressing the hemagglutinin of the first bovine-to-human strain, A/Texas/37/2024, stimulated strong, long-lasting humoral responses and a balanced Th1/Th2 profile in murine studies, providing 100 percent protection against lethal homologous challenge, and produced cross-clade binding antibody responses with a favorable safety profile in rats. Separately, an H5N1 vaccine cultured in serum-free MDCK cell suspension protected mice in challenge tests, with antibodies persisting up to eight months after the first dose in rats and elevated IP-10 levels indicating enhanced innate immunity. The review closes by linking vaccine science to delivery and equity. Intradermal delivery targets the immune cells of the skin and can achieve strong responses with lower antigen doses, extending scarce vaccine supplies, though it requires specialized equipment and trained personnel. Microneedle patches offer needle-free, self-administered vaccination with thermostability that removes cold-chain constraints, although mass production and regulatory licensing remain hurdles. Mucosal intranasal vaccines induce both systemic and mucosal immunity at the respiratory entry point but face stability and formulation issues. Heterologous prime-boost regimens, such as intramuscular priming followed by mucosal boosting, may make immunity more durable and broader against variants. The authors argue that equitable global distribution frameworks such as COVAX must ensure vaccines reach low- and middle-income countries based on need, with high-risk groups prioritized. Combined, they conclude, universal vaccines targeting conserved regions, durable cross-protection, agile manufacturing and fair distribution form the strategy they identify as most capable of reducing the threat of an H5N1 pandemic and improving global preparedness. analysis.brief_en: A review published in Discover Immunity on 4 October 2026 highlights the progress of universal influenza vaccine platforms toward broader H5N1 pandemic readiness. The review emphasizes that H5N1, a highly pathogenic avian influenza virus, is a significant threat due to its antigenic variability and potential for human-to-human transmission. It describes how current vaccines, such as inactivated and recombinant hemagglutinin vaccines, are strain-specific and lack real-world effectiveness data. The review also discusses the development of next-generation vaccines, including mRNA and virus-like particle platforms, which offer faster production and broader immune responses. However, it notes that these vaccines still face challenges in inducing durable, cross-protective immunity against multiple H5N1 variants. The authors stress the need for further research and development to improve vaccine efficacy and address the risks posed by H5N1's rapid mutation rate and expanded host range.

news.source_body_en: A review published in Discover Immunity on 4 October 2026 highlights the progress of universal influenza vaccine platforms toward broader H5N1 pandemic readiness. The review emphasizes that H5N1, a highly pathogenic avian influenza virus, is a significant threat due to its antigenic variability and potential for human-to-human transmission. It describes how current vaccines, such as inactivated and recombinant hemagglutinin vaccines, are strain-specific and lack real-world effectiveness data. The review also discusses the development of next-generation vaccines, including mRNA and virus-like particle platforms, which offer faster production and broader immune responses. The authors stress the need for further research and development to improve vaccine efficacy and address the risks posed by H5N1's rapid mutation rate and expanded host range.
news.content_zh: 2026 年 10 月 4 日在《Discover Immunity》上发表的一篇评论强调了通用流感 疫苗 平台在更广泛的 H5N1 大流行准备方面取得的进展。该审查强调,H5N1(一种 高致病性禽流感 病毒)由于其抗原变异性和人传人 传播 的潜力而构成重大威胁。它描述了当前的 疫苗(例如灭活和重组血凝素 疫苗)如何具有菌株特异性并且缺乏真实世界的有效性数据。该评论还讨论了下一代 疫苗 的开发,包括 mRNA 和病毒样颗粒平台,该平台提供更快的生产和更广泛的 免疫应答。然而,它指出,这些 疫苗 在诱导针对多种 H5N1 变种的持久、交叉保护性免疫力方面仍然面临挑战。作者强调需要进一步研究和开发,以提高 疫苗 功效并解决 H5N1 快速 突变 速率和扩大的 宿主 范围带来的风险。

The vaccine, described in Nature Biotechnology, encodes the hemagglutinin of A/dairy cattle/Texas/24-008749-002/2024, a strain representative of the clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 viruses that have spread through dairy herds in the United States since 2024, causing mastitis and steep drops in milk production. The vaccine was well tolerated, with no obvious adverse effects reported. Because previous studies had detected trace amounts of vaccine-related mRNA in human milk after SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccination, the researchers also tested whether vaccine-derived mRNA could be found in bovine milk. None of the samples from vaccinated animals contained detectable H5 mRNA, indicating that vaccine-derived mRNA was not present at measurable levels in milk after intramuscular administration. Immunologically, the vaccine performed as designed. H5-reactive IgG appeared in serum as early as 21 days after the first dose and rose significantly after the booster, and functional assays confirmed that serum antibodies could neutralize the challenge virus. Hemagglutination inhibition assays showed that antibodies from all four vaccinated animals blocked viral attachment to red blood cells before challenge. H5-reactive IgG was also detected in milk, appearing in only one vaccinated cow after the prime but in all four after the boost, although milk antibody levels were lower than serum levels and declined more rapidly. The researchers could not run neutralization tests on milk because nonspecific inhibitors in milk from unvaccinated animals interfered with the assay. Discover more vaccine Find Vaccines dairy cattle Manage Livestock dairy cows Deep mutational scanning of the viral hemagglutinin revealed that the neutralizing antibodies in vaccinated cow sera targeted antigenic sites A and B on the globular head of the HA protein, near the receptor-binding domain. The amino acid identities at these strongly targeted sites are not highly variable among circulating clade 2.3.4.4b viruses, suggesting the vaccine is well matched to the strains currently infecting dairy cattle. The authors noted that continued surveillance will be needed to detect any future antigenic changes at these sites. After challenge, the differences between the groups were stark. In unvaccinated cows, H5N1 viral RNA in milk from inoculated mammary quarters was first detected one day after inoculation, peaked at two days, and remained detectable throughout the study period. In vaccinated cows, viral RNA levels were significantly lower at multiple time points, with peak titers about 1,000-fold lower than in unvaccinated animals. Most milk samples that tested positive by PCR with a cycle threshold below 35 contained infectious virus, underscoring the relevance of the RNA measurements. Notably, the researchers found evidence that virus migrated from inoculated to uninoculated mammary quarters in two unvaccinated cows, with viral RNA, infectious virus and viral antigen detected in milk and tissue from uninoculated quarters, whereas viral RNA in milk from uninoculated quarters of vaccinated animals remained below the limit of detection. Discover more infectious infecting infection Clinical outcomes tracked the virological results. Unvaccinated cows showed decreased rumen motility and significant drops in milk production beginning two days after inoculation, with a dramatic decline at day three that persisted through much of the monitoring period. Their milk showed severe changes in color and consistency indicative of mastitis, and California mastitis test scores in inoculated quarters consistently indicated moderate to severe inflammation. Vaccinated cows were far less affected on all these measures, and no significant differences in rectal temperature were observed between the groups. At necropsy, inoculated mammary quarters from unvaccinated cows had macroscopic lesion scores of 95.4 percent compared with 8.1 percent in vaccinated cows, and microscopic scoring of collagen staining showed significantly less mammary fibrosis in the vaccinated group. The authors emphasize that the vaccine reduced disease and shedding but did not sterilize infection. While it is reasonable to suspect that the large reduction in viral titers in milk would limit animal-to-animal transmission, they write that additional large-scale field experiments will be required to test that possibility directly. They also note that future work should optimize vaccination schedules and doses, explore whether a single immunization could elicit protective antibody levels in milk, and consider a differentiating infected from vaccinated animals strategy, since the vaccine elicits antibodies only to the hemagglutinin and detection of nucleoprotein antibodies could indicate natural infection. Discover more Get Fresh Dairy Read Med Journals Track Biotech Check Symptoms Study Biology The economic stakes are considerable. The authors cite a study estimating losses of 950 US dollars per clinically affected cow in an infected herd, totaling approximately 737,500 dollars for the herd studied, driven by decreased milk production, mortality and early herd removal. Because the main site of H5N1 replication in cattle is mammary tissue rather than the respiratory tract, and transmission between animals is thought to occur through viral shedding in milk, a vaccine that reduces virus in milk could be particularly valuable for controlling spread within and between farms, while also limiting potential spillovers into humans and other susceptible animals. The authors also note that they did not assess T cell-mediated immunity in this study, although their earlier work in calves found that mRNA–LNP vaccination induces potent CD8+ T cell responses. They conclude that the H5 mRNA–LNP vaccine is safe and immunogenic in lactating dairy cows, eliciting robust antibody responses in serum and milk while reducing clinical disease, virus shedding in milk and mammary gland fibrosis, and they position it as an additional tool to be combined with existing control measures and robust viral testing programs rather than a standalone solution. analysis.time: The study was published on October 28, 2026, and the experimental results were reported as of that date. The challenge study was conducted with a timeline of days post-inoculation.
analysis.location_and_population: The study involved lactating dairy cows in the United States, specifically focusing on a strain of H5N1 that has spread through dairy herds since 2024.
analysis.event: An experimental mRNA–lipid nanoparticle vaccine against H5N1 was tested in lactating dairy cows, showing protection from infection and reducing viral RNA in milk by about 1,000-fold. The vaccine was well tolerated with no adverse effects reported.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The vaccine significantly reduced viral RNA levels in milk, mastitis, and mammary fibrosis in vaccinated cows compared to unvaccinated ones. It did not sterilize infection, but the reduction in viral shedding could limit transmission. The study estimated potential economic losses of $950 per affected cow, totaling $737,500 for the herd studied.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study was a controlled challenge study, and the vaccine's effectiveness was confirmed through viral RNA measurements, antibody responses, and clinical outcomes. However, further large-scale field experiments are needed to assess its impact on animal-to-animal transmission. The authors also suggest optimizing vaccination schedules and doses for better protection.

analysis.brief_en: An experimental mRNA–lipid nanoparticle vaccine against H5N1 influenza virus was tested in lactating dairy cows, showing protection from infection and significantly reducing viral RNA levels in milk by about 1,000-fold. The study, published on October 28, 2026, involved a strain of H5N1 that has spread through U.S. dairy herds since 2024. The vaccine was well tolerated, with no adverse effects reported, and elicited robust antibody responses in both serum and milk. Clinical outcomes indicated that vaccinated cows experienced less severe mastitis and mammary fibrosis compared to unvaccinated ones. While the vaccine reduced disease and shedding, it did not sterilize infection, and the authors emphasized the need for further field experiments to assess its impact on transmission. The study estimated potential economic losses of $950 per affected cow, totaling $737,500 for the herd studied, highlighting the importance of controlling H5N1 in dairy cattle to prevent spillovers into humans and other animals.

The study, published on October 28, 2026, involved a strain of H5N1 that has spread through U.S. dairy herds since 2024. The vaccine was well tolerated, with no adverse effects reported, and elicited robust antibody responses in both serum and milk. Clinical outcomes indicated that vaccinated cows experienced less severe mastitis and mammary fibrosis compared to unvaccinated ones. While the vaccine reduced disease and shedding, it did not sterilize infection, and the authors emphasized the need for further field experiments to assess its impact on transmission. The study estimated potential economic losses of $950 per affected cow, totaling $737,500 for the herd studied, highlighting the importance of controlling H5N1 in dairy cattle to prevent spillovers into humans and other animals.

news.content_title: Bird flu threatens the world’s vultures – and the consequences could spread
news.content: Subscribe news videos images take action earthpedia earthsnap Subscribe Griffon vultures are among the scavenging birds threatened by H5N1 avian influenza. Credit: Shutterstock October 28, 2026 Bird flu threatens the world’s vultures – and the consequences could spread A deadly strain of bird flu is threatening vulnerable vulture populations worldwide, raising concerns about disease spread and ecosystem health. ByAndrei Ionescu Staff Writer Follow Earth on Google Vultures do something nobody else will. They eat what is already dead, often rotten, often crawling with pathogens that would kill most other animals. Their remarkable ability to survive exposure to many dangerous pathogens makes them indispensable to healthy ecosystems. Without vultures, carcasses accumulate, bacteria spread, disease moves up the food chain. They are, in a real sense, the biological sanitation system of the terrestrial world. Now the world’s vultures are facing something their natural defenses cannot reliably protect them against. A recently published letter warns that the H5N1 avian influenza virus poses a catastrophic threat to vulture populations already thinned by poisoning, habitat loss, and persecution. Vultures were already in trouble At least 16 of the world’s 23 vulture species are already of conservation concern. The California condor has fewer than 600 individuals alive, including those in captivity. The Andean condor ranges across a continent but in decreasing numbers. Griffon vultures in southern Europe were considered a conservation success story. None of this provides any buffer against H5N1. The scale of what has already happened is sobering. Thousands of American black vultures and turkey vultures have died across the United States and South America. In southern Europe, the 2022 H5N1 outbreak killed at least 16 adult Griffon vultures across Spain and France and left hundreds of chicks dead at breeding sites. California condors, whose total population had fallen to just 27 birds in 1987, lost roughly 6 percent of their wild population in just six weeks. Bearded vultures in Europe have been affected too. Documentation from Africa and Asia remains sparse, partly because surveillance is limited and partly because vulture numbers there have already declined so severely that detecting further losses is harder. A dangerous feedback loop The letter identifies a feedback loop that makes the situation especially dangerous. Vultures are social and congregate at carcasses – the same places where H5N1-infected animals are most likely to have died. As scavengers, they are resistant to many bacterial pathogens, but H5N1 is different. The virus kills with high efficiency across domestic and wild birds alike. It has now been confirmed in over 48 mammal species worldwide. The loop works like this. More infected animals die in the landscape, producing more contaminated carcasses. Vultures gather at these carcasses and contract the virus. As more vultures die, there are fewer birds to remove the carrion. “The greater the number of infected carcasses, the greater the risk of contagion for the vultures,” Morant said. “Since these carcasses can become sources of infection, a paradox arises: as more vultures die, the capacity to eliminate the carrion reduces, the pathogens spread and contagion increases.” What makes this particularly alarming is that many vulture species are already living close to the edge. A virus that kills 6 percent of a California condor population in six weeks is not a manageable mortality event for a species with a few hundred wild individuals. Such losses could undo decades of conservation progress. Tracking outbreaks before they spread The letter proposes five coordinated responses. These are framed explicitly as a guide for conservation managers and policymakers across the diverse range of countries where vultures survive. The first and most urgent is population monitoring. Without knowing where birds are dying and at what rate, it is impossible to calibrate any other response. Migratory species – which cross national borders and carry the virus with them – need particular attention. “In the Basque Country, the Griffon vulture population is in a healthy condition, but the Egyptian vulture is more sensitive. We need to pay particular attention to migratory species,” Morant said. The second is vaccination, where logistical conditions allow. In response to the acute threat to California condors, researchers have already implemented a vaccination program. The letter advocates continuous evaluation of vaccination as populations come under serious risk. Third, feeding stations – a conservation tool widely used for vultures across Europe and parts of Africa – need to be managed so that the carcasses provided are verified free of H5N1. These stations are, by design, places where large numbers of birds aggregate. In the context of a highly contagious pathogen, that aggregation becomes a liability unless the food supply is controlled. Biosecurity protocols and context-specific actions Fourth, researchers working with vultures must follow strict biosecurity protocols since the virus can persist in feathers and tissue after death. Fifth, the letter calls for context-specific national action plans embedded in shared cross-border governance frameworks. The countries that host significant vulture populations range across vastly different socioeconomic contexts and regulatory environments. A one-size approach will not work. But the absence of coordination across borders will not work either, given that the birds themselves do not recognize frontiers. Why vultures cannot recover quickly Vulture populations once collapsed can take decades to recover, if they recover at all. The birds are long-lived and slow to reproduce – most species raise only one chick per year. A sustained mortality event can hollow out a population without any dramatic visible collapse, simply by preventing the replacement of birds that die. H5N1 adds rapid, acute mortality on top of that slow demographic pressure. “We wanted to alert the research community and those responsible for conservation so that they could establish coordinated actions,” Morant said. “To tackle this dangerous epidemiological situation, it is urgent to develop coordinated cross-border plans and to integrate these actions into shared governance structures.” The birds that clean up after everything else now need someone to look after them. The study is published in the journal Conservation Biology. — Like what you read? Subscribe to our newsletter for engaging articles, exclusive content, and the latest updates.
