H5N1病毒近期在美国泌乳奶牛中暴发,主要引起乳腺炎与产奶量骤降。该病毒主要复制场所为乳腺组织而非呼吸道,动物间传播被认为通过乳汁中病毒排出实现。研究人员构建了一种编码A/dairy cattle/Tex 欢迎免费下载技术干货《重组蛋白表达过程中遇到的问题及解决方案!》 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 Article Open access 高致病性禽流感(HPAI)clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1病毒近期在美国泌乳奶牛中暴发,主要引起乳腺炎与产奶量骤降。该病毒主要复制场所为乳腺组织而非呼吸道,动物间传播被认为通过乳汁中病毒排出实现。研究人员构建了一种编码A/dairy cattle/Texas/24-008749-002/2024株血凝素(HA)的mRNA–脂质纳米颗粒(mRNA–LNP)疫苗,并在泌乳奶牛中评估其免疫原性与保护效力。实验将8头奶牛分为疫苗组与对照组,分别接受两剂肌肉注射疫苗或生理盐水,随后进行乳腺内病毒攻毒。接种可在血清中诱导体液免疫,产生HA反应性抗体与中和抗体,并在乳汁中检出HA反应性抗体。攻毒后,疫苗组乳汁中病毒RNA峰值降低约1000倍,乳腺炎与乳腺纤维化发生率显著下降。结果表明,该mRNA–LNP疫苗可高效抑制乳腺内H5N1复制并减轻临床损伤,为奶牛禽流感防控提供新策略。 论文解读:H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b mRNA–LNP疫苗保护泌乳奶牛抵御乳腺内感染的研究进展 点击免费下载【综合性的体外药效评价解决方案】,全方位支持您的抗体药研发项目,快速地完成体外药效试验以及获得优质药效的先导分子。领 取 研究背景与立项依据 高致病性禽流感(HPAI,highly pathogenic avian influenza)clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1病毒自2024年起在美国奶牛群中持续传播,造成泌乳奶牛严重乳腺炎、产奶量断崖式下降及重大经济损失。与典型流感不同,该病毒不主要侵袭呼吸道,而是特异嗜性乳腺分泌上皮,病毒经乳汁排出成为牛群内传播核心环节;同时跨种传播至人群的风险引发公共卫生关切。现有防控依赖生物安全与管理,缺乏针对泌乳奶牛、面向乳腺局部保护的高效疫苗。因此,研究人员拟验证一种编码流行株HA的核苷修饰mRNA–脂质纳米颗粒(mRNA–LNP)疫苗能否在奶牛体内诱导系统性与泌乳腺局部免疫,并阻断乳腺内感染与病毒脱落。 主要技术方法概述 研究纳入宾夕法尼亚州HPAI监测阴性荷斯坦泌乳奶牛8头(2–8岁),分疫苗组与盐水对照组各4头,采用prime–boost肌注免疫。关键方法包括:定量PCR(qPCR)检测乳中疫苗mRNA残留;酶联免疫吸附试验(ELISA)测血清与乳中HA特异性IgG;焦点减少中和试验(FRNT)与血凝抑制试验(HAI)评估功能抗体;基于假病毒深度突变扫描(deep mutational scanning)定位血清中和表位;乳腺内接种同源H5N1病毒攻毒;RT–qPCR监测多样本病毒RNA;加州乳腺炎试验(CMT)与组织学天狼星红染色评估宏观/微观纤维化;免疫组化(IHC)检测病毒核蛋白(NP)抗原。 研究结果 H5 mRNA–LNP疫苗在泌乳奶牛中安全性良好 研究人员在首免与加强后连续采集乳汁,以高灵敏qPCR检测疫苗来源H5 mRNA,下限为65拷贝/μl,结果所有乳样均未检出疫苗mRNA,证明肌注后疫苗核酸不向乳汁可检测性转移,对乳品安全与奶牛本身均无直接残留风险。 H5 mRNA–LNP疫苗在泌乳奶牛中具有强免疫原性 接种后21天即可见HA特异性IgG上升,加强后显著升高;FRNT显示血清具备高效中和能力,HAI证实抗体可阻断红细胞凝集。乳汁中加强后亦出现HA反应性IgG,但滴度低于血清且衰减更快。少数动物入组前存在低水平交叉反应IgG,归因于人流感H1暴露,不影响疫苗应答。 疫苗诱导抗体的表位特异性 借助假病毒深度突变扫描,研究人员发现中和抗体集中识别HA球状头区抗原位点A与B(邻近受体结合域),这些位点在circulating clade 2.3.4.4b病毒中高度保守,提示该疫苗诱导的免疫压力不易被当前流行株逃逸。 H5 mRNA–LNP接种保护泌乳奶牛抵御H5N1感染 乳腺内攻毒后,对照组乳中病毒RNA于第2天达峰并持续阳性;疫苗组接种乳区病毒RNA峰值降低约1000倍,多时间点显著更低,且未接种乳区病毒扩散受限。鼻眼拭子、血液等样本中疫苗组检出极少。产奶量方面,对照组自攻毒后第2–3天骤降且长期不能恢复,疫苗组下降轻微;反刍活动亦受保护。乳腺炎评分(颜色、黏稠度、CMT)显示疫苗组几乎无中重度炎症。 疫苗显著降低乳腺纤维化 剖检与组织学分析表明,对照组接种乳区宏观病变评分95.4% vs 疫苗组8.1%;天狼星红染色显示疫苗组小叶内与叶间胶原沉积明显减少,微观纤维化评分更低,有效遏制坏死性乳腺炎后的纤维替代。 讨论与结论翻译 讨论指出,clade 2.3.4.4b在牛群的经济损失每名临床牛约950美元,疫苗联合检测可压低传播与跨种风险。本研究系统量化了mRNA–LNP对乳腺内感染的防护:不仅降病毒载量,还保产奶、减纤维化。乳汁抗体虽低于血清,但局部中和潜力存在;未来需优化免疫程序、单剂持久性、DIVA(区分感染与接种动物)策略。表位保守性支持该平台匹配当前流行株,且既往研究提示可辅以T细胞免疫防逃逸。 研究结论部分译述如下: 综上,H5 mRNA–LNP 2.3.4.4b疫苗在泌乳奶牛中安全、免疫原性明确,可于血清与乳汁诱导强健HA抗体;攻毒后显著削弱临床疾病(尤其产奶损失),大幅降低乳中病毒脱落与乳腺纤维化。该疫苗可作为现行管控措施之外的补充工具,用于抑制农场内暴发、降低场间传播并缓解乳业经济损害。 你想把这篇解读压缩成投稿用的“审稿意见摘要”,还是会议汇报用的“研究亮点”? 审稿摘要 研究亮点 审稿摘要 研究亮点 打赏 Article Open access 高致病性禽流感(HPAI)clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1病毒近期在美国泌乳奶牛中暴发,主要引起乳腺炎与产奶量骤降。该病毒主要复制场所为乳腺组织而非呼吸道,动物间传播被认为通过乳汁中病毒排出实现。研究人员构建了一种编码A/dairy cattle/Texas/24-008749-002/2024株血凝素(HA)的mRNA–脂质纳米颗粒(mRNA–LNP)疫苗,并在泌乳奶牛中评估其免疫原性与保护效力。实验将8头奶牛分为疫苗组与对照组,分别接受两剂肌肉注射疫苗或生理盐水,随后进行乳腺内病毒攻毒。接种可在血清中诱导体液免疫,产生HA反应性抗体与中和抗体,并在乳汁中检出HA反应性抗体。攻毒后,疫苗组乳汁中病毒RNA峰值降低约1000倍,乳腺炎与乳腺纤维化发生率显著下降。结果表明,该mRNA–LNP疫苗可高效抑制乳腺内H5N1复制并减轻临床损伤,为奶牛禽流感防控提供新策略。 H5N1病毒自2024年起在美国奶牛群中持续传播,造成泌乳奶牛严重乳腺炎、产奶量断崖式下降及重大经济损失。与典型流感不同,该病毒不主要侵袭呼吸道,而是特异嗜性乳腺分泌上皮,病毒经乳汁排出成为牛群内传播核心环节;同时跨种传播至人群的风险引发公共卫生关切。现有防控依赖生物安全与管理,缺乏针对泌乳奶牛、面向乳腺局部保护的高效疫苗。因此,研究人员拟验证一种编码流行株HA的核苷修饰mRNA–脂质纳米颗粒(mRNA–LNP)疫苗能否在奶牛体内诱导系统性与泌乳腺局部免疫,并阻断乳腺内感染与病毒脱落。 主要技术方法概述 研究纳入宾夕法尼亚州HPAI监测阴性荷斯坦泌乳奶牛8头(2–8岁),分疫苗组与盐水对照组各4头,采用prime–boost肌注免疫。关键方法包括:定量PCR(qPCR)检测乳中疫苗mRNA残留;酶联免疫吸附试验(ELISA)测血清与乳中HA特异性IgG;焦点减少中和试验(FRNT)与血凝抑制试验(HAI)评估功能抗体;基于假病毒深度突变扫描(deep mutational scanning)定位血清中和表位;乳腺内接种同源H5N1病毒攻毒;RT–qPCR监测多样本病毒RNA;加州乳腺炎试验(CMT)与组织学天狼星红染色评估宏观/微观纤维化;免疫组化(IHC)检测病毒核蛋白(NP)抗原。 研究结果 H5 mRNA–LNP疫苗在泌乳奶牛中安全性良好 研究人员在首免与加强后连续采集乳汁,以高灵敏qPCR检测疫苗来源H5 mRNA,下限为65拷贝/μl,结果所有乳样均未检出疫苗mRNA,证明肌注后疫苗核酸不向乳汁可检测性转移,对乳品安全与奶牛本身均无直接残留风险。 H5 mRNA–LNP疫苗在泌乳奶牛中具有强免疫原性 接种后21天即可见HA特异性IgG上升,加强后显著升高;FRNT显示血清具备高效中和能力,HAI证实抗体可阻断红细胞凝集。乳汁中加强后亦出现HA反应性IgG,但滴度低于血清且衰减更快。少数动物入组前存在低水平交叉反应IgG,归因于人流感H1暴露,不影响疫苗应答。 疫苗诱导抗体的表位特异性 借助假病毒深度突变扫描,研究人员发现中和抗体集中识别HA球状头区抗原位点A与B(邻近受体结合域),这些位点在circulating clade 2.3.4.4b病毒中高度保守,提示该疫苗诱导的免疫压力不易被当前流行株逃逸。 H5 mRNA–LNP接种保护泌乳奶牛抵御H5N1感染 乳腺内攻毒后,对照组乳中病毒RNA于第2天达峰并持续阳性;疫苗组接种乳区病毒RNA峰值降低约1000倍,多时间点显著更低,且未接种乳区病毒扩散受限。鼻眼拭子、血液等样本中疫苗组检出极少。产奶量方面,对照组自攻毒后第2–3天骤降且长期不能恢复,疫苗组下降轻微;反刍活动亦受保护。乳腺炎评分(颜色、黏稠度、CMT)显示疫苗组几乎无中重度炎症。 疫苗显著降低乳腺纤维化 剖检与组织学分析表明,对照组接种乳区宏观病变评分95.4% vs 疫苗组8.1%;天狼星红染色显示疫苗组小叶内与叶间胶原沉积明显减少,微观纤维化评分更低,有效遏制坏死性乳腺炎后的纤维替代。 讨论与结论翻译 讨论指出,clade 2.3.4.4b在牛群的经济损失每名临床牛约950美元,疫苗联合检测可压低传播与跨种风险。本研究系统量化了mRNA–LNP对乳腺内感染的防护:不仅降病毒载量,还保产奶、减纤维化。乳汁抗体虽低于血清,但局部中和潜力存在;未来需优化免疫程序、单剂持久性、DIVA(区分感染与接种动物)策略。表位保守性支持该平台匹配当前流行株,且既往研究提示可辅以T细胞免疫防逃逸。 研究结论部分译述如下: 综上,H5 mRNA–LNP 2.3.4.4b疫苗在泌乳奶牛中安全、免疫原性明确,可于血清与乳汁诱导强健HA抗体;攻毒后显著削弱临床疾病(尤其产奶损失),大幅降低乳中病毒脱落与乳腺纤维化。该疫苗可作为现行管控措施之外的补充工具,用于抑制农场内暴发、降低场间传播并缓解乳业经济损害。 你想把这篇解读压缩成投稿用的“审稿意见摘要”,还是会议汇报用的“研究亮点”? 审稿摘要 研究亮点 审稿摘要 研究亮点 打赏 news.content_title: Trump administration loses grip on bird flu, experts warn
news.content: The Trump administration has been criticised for losing control of a bird flu outbreak that has spread among mink and cattle farms across the United States. The H5N1 virus has infected around 1,000 people since it was first detected in the late 1990s, killing roughly half of them. While it currently does not spread among humans, scientists have long worried that it could trigger a pandemic, and that each human infection raises the risk of the virus mutating. A new variant emerged in 2020 and has since spread to millions of birds and hundreds of animal species across the globe, leading to devastating losses in both wildlife and farmed livestock and poultry. While some countries have introduced tough measures to curb its spread, including mandatory culls of infected animals, "flockdowns" (where birds are kept indoors) and vaccination of farm workers who handle at-risk livestock, experts say the US is allowing the virus to run rampant. For more than two months, an outbreak has raged unchecked on a Utah farm that raises thousands of mink for fur, news outlet ProPublica reported last week. Mink in captivity have previously been described as pandemic "time bombs". The size and density of the farms give invading viruses a perfect environment in which to mutate . Mink have very similar respiratory systems to humans, increasing the risk that a virus can spread between the animals and people, and undergo a process known as "reassortment", when two or more viruses mix together to make a new, more dangerous strain. H5N1 is now endemic in US farmed cows - AFP via Getty Images/RONALDO SCHEMIDT Despite calls for the animals to be culled, state officials have refused to mandate any action, ProPublica revealed. Reports suggest Utah state officials are prioritising the financial interests of the fur trade, most of which is exported to China and Russia, and that federal officials have failed to intervene. Outbreaks of H5N1 in farmed mink in Spain and Finland have resulted in mass culls, and several countries, including Britain and, just last week, Denmark, historically the largest producer of mink fur in the world, have banned mink farming over its disease risks. "I can't completely wrap my head around it. And you still have workers going into the mink farm, and it's flu season, so this is when there's a chance for new recombinants to occur," Marc Johnson, a virologist at the University of Missouri, told The Telegraph. It's not just the mink outbreak that is concerning scientists. H5N1 'jumped' from birds into dairy cattle in late 2023 and is now endemic in US farmed cows. Experts say the outbreak is not only costing the dairy industry millions of dollars, but also raises the risk that the virus could mutate to spread more easily between mammals. More than 700 herds across dozens of states have now been infected with H5N1. While it rarely causes death in cattle, it can cause severe illness and lead to lower milk yield. Each new infection also raises the risk to humans. At least 72 people have caught H5N1 in the US since 2024, mostly through working with sick dairy cattle. Last week the US recorded its first case of H5N1 this year in a farm worker from Washington. Experts say deep cuts to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the agency responsible for managing human health threats, and to the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) have weakened efforts to contain it. "A year ago, we heard that the federal workers responsible for controlling the dairy outbreak had been fired," said Dr Jennifer Nuzzo, professor of epidemiology and director of the pandemic centre at Brown University School of Public Health, whose team originally helped manage the outbreak. "We haven't heard much since then about what's going on, nor what has been restored, or whether testing programmes are ongoing." Federal officials and disease experts like Dr Nuzzo used to hold frequent calls. "The calls were an opportunity for us to say, 'Have you considered this approach?' and to ask why they were taking certain actions," she said. The calls no longer happen, which she called "a great loss". "The virus is still in birds, but the cow [outbreak] is completely preventable," said Dr Johnson. "Cattle infections last only a few weeks before the animals recover. If infected herds were simply isolated until the outbreak fizzled out, it would stop. "But cattle keep being moved around, spreading it into new states," said Dr Johnson, referring to the way the US dairy industry operates, in which cows are routinely transported across state lines, whether to join new herds, for breeding, or to replace animals at large milk-producing operations. Experts are calling on the government to introduce stricter biosecurity measures on farms, regulate the movement of cattle between states, and help to support better personal protection for farmworkers. Last year, the Trump administration also pulled the plug on a $766 million contract awarded to Moderna that would help to develop a human H5N1 vaccine, citing concerns over mRNA technology. "The cancellation [of the contract] means that the government is discarding what could be one of the most effective and rapid tools to combat an avian influenza outbreak," Amesh Adalja, senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health, said at the time. Read more → October 24, 2026 The sweeter side of veterinary medicine Vet Candy | Free Veterinary CE, News & NAVLE Prep We make learning fun! ‍ ‍ ‍ Welcome to your new favorite place to grow in vet med. Discover brilliant experts, engaging videos, interactive quizzes, inspiring stories, and podcasts that keep you curious, connected, and excited about what's next. JOIN US EXPLORE Frequently Asked Questions About Vet Candy What is Vet Candy? Vet Candy is a free veterinary media and education platform serving 50,000+ veterinary professionals. We create podcasts, CE content, NAVLE prep resources, a digital magazine, career tools, and original editorial — all built for the veterinary professionals who want to stay sharp, stay connected, and actually enjoy the ride. Is Vet Candy really free? Yes. Membership is completely free. No credit card, no trial period, no catch. Join once and access everything — podcasts, articles, CE on demand, NAVLE Warriors, Rising Stars, Career Club, and more. Who is Vet Candy for? Vet Candy is for veterinary professionals at every stage — vet students grinding through preclinical years, new graduates figuring out their first job, practicing DVMs looking to stay current, vet techs building their careers, and anyone else who chose this profession and wants to feel good about that choice. What is NAVLE Warriors? NAVLE Warriors is Vet Candy's flagship exam prep program — a structured, strategic resource built to help vet students pass the NAVLE on the first attempt. Tuskegee University CVM used NAVLE Warriors and their pass rate improved from 51% to 74% in a single year. It is free for all Vet Candy members. What is Vet Candy Match? Vet Candy Match is a free career guidance program for veterinary professionals who are ready to find a job that actually fits. The program covers self-discovery, career planning, resume and cover letter building, and interview prep — and connects candidates with real placement opportunities through Vet Candy's partnership with Hopper Vets. It is free for all veterinary professionals. What podcasts does Vet Candy produce? Vet Candy is the number one veterinary podcast on Apple. Our shows include Brain Smarts — a science and trivia game show hosted by Clay and Caitlin Palmer — Cat Daddy, the ultimate feline trivia showdown, Let's Be Honest, which covers the real and unfiltered side of veterinary medicine, and 21 Questions, which introduces the veterinary professionals worth knowing. New episodes drop regularly. What is Vet Candy Magazine? Vet Candy Magazine is a free digital publication featuring cover stories on veterinary professionals, clinical insights, lifestyle content, and original reporting on the issues that matter most in vet med. It is published multiple times per year and available free at myvetcandy.com/magazines. What is Vet Candy Rising Stars? Rising Stars is Vet Candy's annual program celebrating veterinary students and early-career DVMs who are already making an impact in the profession. Each honoree receives a full editorial feature, social media coverage, and recognition across the Vet Candy platform. The 2026 class is live now at myvetcandy.com/rising-stars. What CE does Vet Candy offer? Vet Candy offers RACE approved on demand continuing education We have Master Courses, talk shows, Endocrinology Secrets and Dermatology Secrets programs, featuring board-certified veterinary specialists. CE credits are available for licensed veterinary professionals. Visit myvetcandy.com/ce-on-demand to browse current offerings. Who founded Vet Candy? Vet Candy was founded by Dr. Jill López, DVM, MBA — a veterinarian, entrepreneur, and Tuskegee University CVM graduate with a background in pharmaceutical industry work at Merck Animal Health and consulting at the ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center. She built Vet Candy as a community-first media brand and it has grown to become the leading platform for the next generation of veterinary professionals. How do I join Vet Candy? Visit myvetcandy.com/join. Membership is free, takes less than two minutes, and gives you immediate access to everything on the platform. Where can I find veterinary magazines that provide clinical updates and expert advice? Vet Candy offers engaging, easy-to-digest veterinary content that includes clinical insights, expert advice, and the latest trends in animal health. Our digital magazine and content platform are designed to keep veterinarians and veterinary professionals informed while making learning enjoyable and accessible. Where can I find free, RACE-approved continuing education courses for veterinarians? Vet Candy provides free, RACE-approved continuing education (CE) courses created with leading experts in the veterinary field. These courses are designed to help veterinarians stay current with clinical best practices while earning CE credits in a convenient, on-demand format. Are there any free membership platforms offering resources and community support for veterinary professionals? Yes—Vet Candy offers a free membership platform where veterinary professionals can access exclusive content, educational resources, career tools, and a supportive community. Members also get access to special events, expert-led discussions, and industry insights. What are the best resources for NAVLE exam preparation for veterinary students? Vet Candy offers NAVLE preparation resources designed specifically for veterinary students. These include educational content, review materials, and expert-led guidance to help students feel confident and prepared for the exam

Photograph: Alexandros Avramidis/Reuters Bird flu outbreak at Utah mink farm sparks concerns about government response State veterinarian attempted to get help from federal government but was told USDA didn’t regulate mink farms An outbreak of bird flu at a mink farm in Utah – and the response from its owner and regulators – has sparked concerns from infectious disease experts about the Trump administration’s ability to manage such viruses. While the mink becoming sick was unlikely to produce a “tidal wave of human infections”, an apparent lack of transparency from government officials about the infections was very troubling, said Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiology professor and director of the pandemic center at Brown University School of Public Health. “No animal or human will be protected from the toll of this virus through secrecy,” Nuzzo said in a phone interview on Saturday. “The risk is greatest among people who have exposure to sick animals. If that is not you, I think you can take this off your worry list, [but] it does not abdicate the government of its responsibility to try to prevent a pandemic.” ‘The silence was the worst part’: after culling his entire flock, US poultry farmer now fears bird flu Read more For two months, an outbreak of bird flu has spread at a farm about an hour from Salt Lake City that raises thousands of mink for their fur, ProPublica reported earlier this week. A state veterinarian, Amanda Price, handled the response and tried to get help from the US Department of Agriculture (USDA), but the federal officials told her that they didn’t regulate mink or have a vaccine approved for the animal, according to ProPublica, which obtained messages through the state’s public records law. The USDA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) officials spoke with Utah health department staff but did not communicate with Price, the outlet further reported. In other countries where such outbreaks have occurred, the government has ordered farms to kill their mink. Veterinarians told ProPublica that is what the Utah farm owners should already have done. This is not the first outbreak in recent times at a Utah fur farm. During the Covid-19 pandemic, nearly 10,000 mink in Utah died from the coronavirus and quarantines were implemented at nine farms. The virus was probably transmitted to the animals from infected workers, according to a report in the journal Emerging Infectious Diseases. Mink are very susceptible to infection with several viruses that also infect humans, according to a report from the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. But Nuzzo said she didn’t “see any signals that the virus is spreading”. “The scenario I’m worried about is this one: workers who are exposed to these animals will get sick, and some of them might die, and that is awful because we potentially could prevent that through thinking about protecting farm workers with a vaccine, like other countries are using,” Nuzzo said. The virus could infect humans and become a pandemic if it were to combine with an influenza virus, “a worry that grows with the onset of each human flu season when there are more influenza viruses in circulation”, Nuzzo said. “I cannot tell you what the probability of that is. It could be zero,” she added. In Utah, a fur trade representative told Price that culling the mink at C&T Fenn Farms would kill the business and the industry, ProPublica reported. But Tom Peacock, an avian influenza researcher at the Pirbright Institute, told the news organization that in such situations, depopulation – ie, culling the mink – typically happens quickly and the fact that it didn’t in this case was “very concerning”. Officials reportedly also did not monitor the farm workers for symptoms, despite CDC guidance to do so. ProPublica found two people who worked at the farm, one of whom had a red eye. The federal health agency urges testing for that symptom. Price and the Utah department of agriculture and food did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The farm owner, Chad Fenn, told the news organization that the worker had dust in his eye and that the state health department did not recommend testing. The Guardian could not immediately reach Fenn. Nuzzo worries about how, she said, during Donald Trump’s second term, the federal government appears to be doing less monitoring of farms for such potential viruses than previous administrations. Shortly after Trump took office, his administration fired federal employees who were responding to a bird flu outbreak among dairy cows. Nuzzo said federal officials used to hold regular calls with disease experts such as her to “keep us informed about what they were doing”. That no longer happens, she said. “I found them quite useful because it allowed us to push them and say, ‘Well, what about this?’, and to interrogate some of the ideas,” Nuzzo said. “A lot is lost when that doesn’t happen ... It might mean that things are going on that people don’t see or know about. It might also be that actions don’t get the scrutiny they deserve.” Explore more on these topics Utah Bird flu Trump administration Infectious diseases Health features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Visit Norway makes shithouses ‘great again’ after Trump insult The low-budget Brewers won the World Series – and exposed baseball’s biggest lieHoward Bryant Patrick Stewart, Star Trek actor and acclaimed thespian, dies aged 86 Patrick Stewart: the legacy of domestic violence Live Trump again calls for prosecution of Mary Peltola as turmoil grows over Alaska campaign investigation – live Most viewed Most viewed

In other countries where such outbreaks have occurred, the government has ordered farms to kill their mink. Veterinarians told ProPublica that is what the Utah farm owners should already have done. This is not the first outbreak in recent times at a Utah fur farm. During the Covid-19 pandemic, nearly 10,000 mink in Utah died from the coronavirus and quarantines were implemented at nine farms. The virus was probably transmitted to the animals from infected workers, according to a report in the journal Emerging Infectious Diseases. Mink are very susceptible to infection with several viruses that also infect humans, according to a report from the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. But Nuzzo said she didn’t “see any signals that the virus is spreading”. “The scenario I’m worried about is this one: workers who are exposed to these animals will get sick, and some of them might die, and that is awful because we potentially could prevent that through thinking about protecting farm workers with a vaccine, like other countries are using,” Nuzzo said. The virus could infect humans and become a pandemic if it were to combine with an influenza virus, “a worry that grows with the onset of each human flu season when there are more influenza viruses in circulation”, Nuzzo said. “I cannot tell you what the probability of that is. It could be zero,” she added. In Utah, a fur trade representative told Price that culling the mink at C&T Fenn Farms would kill the business and the industry, ProPublica reported. But Tom Peacock, an avian influenza researcher at the Pirbright Institute, told the news organization that in such situations, depopulation – ie, culling the mink – typically happens quickly and the fact that it didn’t in this case was “very concerning”. Officials reportedly also did not monitor the farm workers for symptoms, despite CDC guidance to do so. ProPublica found two people who worked at the farm, one of whom had a red eye. The federal health agency urges testing for that symptom. Price and the Utah department of agriculture and food did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The farm owner, Chad Fenn, told the news organization that the worker had dust in his eye and that the state health department did not recommend testing. The Guardian could not immediately reach Fenn. Nuzzo worries about how, she said, during Donald Trump’s second term, the federal government appears to be doing less monitoring of farms for such potential viruses than previous administrations. Shortly after Trump took office, his administration fired federal employees who were responding to a bird flu outbreak among dairy cows. Nuzzo said federal officials used to hold regular calls with disease experts such as her to “keep us informed about what they were doing”. That no longer happens, she said. “I found them quite useful because it allowed us to push them and say, ‘Well, what about this?’, and to interrogate some of the ideas,” Nuzzo said. “A lot is lost when that doesn’t happen ... It might mean that things are going on that people don’t see or know about. news.content_zh: 犹他州一家水貂养殖场爆发的禽流感 暴发 引发了人们对政府反应的担忧,特别是在特朗普政府的领导下。州兽医阿曼达·普莱斯 (Amanda Price) 试图向美国农业部寻求联邦援助,但被告知水貂养殖场不受监管,并且没有 疫苗 获得批准用于这些动物。虽然 暴发 并未导致人类确诊病例,但詹妮弗·努佐 (Jennifer Nuzzo) 等专家警告农场工人存在潜在风险,他们可能会从受感染的水貂身上感染病毒。州和联邦官员之间缺乏透明度和沟通,引发了人们对政府管理此类 暴发 准备情况的担忧。此外,美国农业部没有回应置评请求,农场主查德·芬恩 (Chad Fenn) 提到,这名工人的眼睛里有灰尘,但不建议进行测试。努佐还对特朗普政府期间对农场的监控比以前减少表示担忧,强调需要加强监督以防止潜在的流行病。

Bob Conrad / THIS IS RENO By ThisIsReno Nevada wildlife and public health officials have confirmed an outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza, commonly known as bird flu, among multiple flocks of geese in the Reno-Sparks area. Geese at the University of Nevada, Reno were confirmed to be impacted. UNR President Brian Sandoval, in a campus email, said campus geese were confirmed sick. “The University is aware of sick and deceased geese observed near Manzanita Lake and is coordinating with NDOW,” Sandoval wrote. “The risk of infection to the general public is considered low, but people should avoid direct contact with sick or dead wild birds and keep pets and children away from them.” The Nevada Department of Wildlife, Nevada Department of Agriculture and Nevada Division of Public and Behavioral Health are coordinating their response to the outbreak. Officials are asking residents to report sick geese and take precautions when encountering dead birds to help prevent the virus from spreading. Highly pathogenic avian influenza is a contagious virus that affects wild birds and domestic poultry. It can also infect livestock and humans, although transmission to people is rare. Signs of infection in birds include coughing, sneezing, discharge from the eyes or nose, swelling around the eyes, poor balance, abnormal head or neck positioning, diarrhea, weakness and sudden death. Residents who encounter sick geese should leave the birds alone, keep children and pets away and report their location to the Nevada Department of Wildlife at 775-688-1500. People who find dead geese in public parks should contact the agency responsible for the property. Reno residents can reach city parks officials at 775-334-2270, while Washoe County Parks can be contacted at 775-828-6612. For dead waterfowl found on private property, officials recommend wearing gloves, an N95 mask and eye protection when handling the birds. Carcasses should be double-bagged and placed in municipal trash. Residents who own poultry should change their clothing and shoes after encountering a dead goose to reduce the risk of transmitting the virus to their flocks. State officials are also urging backyard poultry owners to keep their birds in secure enclosures away from wild waterfowl, disinfect equipment, store feed securely and monitor their flocks for signs of illness. Poultry are particularly vulnerable to the virus, with mortality rates potentially exceeding 90%, according to the Department of Wildlife. Wild waterfowl may carry the virus without showing symptoms, although some species of geese, raptors and game birds can experience significant illness and death. Poultry owners who notice unusual illness or unexpected deaths should contact a veterinarian. High mortality rates among domestic poultry should be reported to the Nevada Department of Agriculture at diseasereporting@agri.nv.gov. Although human infections are rare, exposure can occur through contact with infected animals, carcasses or contaminated surfaces without appropriate protective equipment. Symptoms in humans can include fever, cough, sore throat, difficulty breathing, eye irritation, headaches, body aches, congestion, diarrhea and vomiting. Officials advise anyone who develops symptoms after contact with a sick or dead bird to contact a health care provider and disclose the potential exposure. Additional information about bird flu is available through the Nevada Department of Wildlife and Nevada Department of Agriculture. Source: Nevada Department of Wildlife UPDATE: This article was updated to include new information about the UNR geese being infected. news.content: Bird flu has been detected in a Sac County, Iowa, commercial turkey flock. (Photo by Stephen Ausmus/USDA) A case of highly pathogenic avian influenza has been detected in a commercial turkey flock of approximately 44,400 birds in Sac County, according to the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship. While the HPAI H5N1 outbreak has been ongoing since February 2022, Iowa has not reported an outbreak of the bird flu in a commercial flock since December 2025 . The state has reported seven outbreaks of the virus in backyard, mixed species or game bird flocks in 2026. Iowa has had more total birds affected by the bird flu than any other state since the start of the outbreak, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. Gov. Kim Reynolds issued a disaster proclamation for Sac County Wednesday after IDALS's announcement. The disaster proclamation allows state and department resources to be more easily deployed to help contain and monitor the outbreak, which typically requires dispatching the affected flock and disposing of the dead birds. IDALS is encouraging producers and backyard flock owners to "continue bolstering" biosecurity measures to protect their flocks. HPAI is a viral disease that can travel in wild birds and infect wild and domestic birds. Instances of the virus typically rise during bird migration seasons. Poultry producers must report possible cases of the bird flu to IDALS and should contact their veterinarians if they suspect birds with the virus. Some clinical signs include a sudden increase in bird deaths, lethargy, decreased egg production, swelling of head, difficulty breathing, thin-shelled or misshapen eggs and diarrhea. Poultry and egg products remain safe to eat and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, continue to rate the public health risk of bird flu as low as there is no known person-to-person spread. analysis.time: The bird flu outbreak in the commercial turkey flock was detected in Sac County, Iowa, in 2026, with the state having not reported such an outbreak since December 2025. The outbreak has been ongoing since February 2022.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak occurred in Sac County, Iowa, affecting a commercial turkey flock of approximately 44,400 birds. Department of Agriculture and the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship are involved in monitoring and responding to the outbreak.
analysis.event: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) was detected in a commercial turkey flock in Sac County, Iowa, marking the first such outbreak in nearly a year. The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship reported the case.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Iowa has had more total birds affected by bird flu than any other state since the start of the outbreak. In 2026, the state reported seven outbreaks of the virus in backyard, mixed species, or game bird flocks. The public health risk is rated as low by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, as there is no known person-to-person spread.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Kim Reynolds issued a disaster proclamation for Sac County to facilitate the deployment of state and department resources to contain and monitor the outbreak. The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship is encouraging producers and backyard flock owners to bolster biosecurity measures. The outbreak is being managed with standard containment procedures, including the dispatching and disposal of affected flocks.

analysis.brief_en: In Sac County, Iowa, a commercial turkey flock of approximately 44,400 birds was found to be infected with highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1, marking the first such outbreak in nearly a year. The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship reported the case, which has been ongoing since February 2022. Iowa has had more total birds affected by bird flu than any other state since the outbreak began, with seven outbreaks reported in 2026 involving backyard, mixed species, or game bird flocks. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention continue to rate the public health risk as low, as there is no known person-to-person transmission. In response, Kim Reynolds issued a disaster proclamation to allow for easier deployment of resources to contain and monitor the outbreak, which typically involves dispatching the affected flock and disposing of dead birds. The state is urging producers and backyard flock owners to enhance biosecurity measures to prevent further spread.

news.content_zh: 在爱荷华州萨克县,大约 44,400 只火鸡群被发现感染了 高致病性禽流感 (HPAI) H5N1,这是近一年来首次出现此类 高致病性禽流感。爱荷华州农业和土地管理部报告了这一案件,该案件自 2022 年 2 月以来一直在进行中。自 暴发 启动以来,爱荷华州受禽流感影响的鸟类总数比任何其他州都多,2026 年报告了 7 起 暴发 事件,涉及后院、混合物种或猎禽群。美国疾病控制与预防中心继续将公共卫生风险评级为低,因为没有已知的人与人之间的 传播。作为回应,Kim Reynolds 发布了一份灾难公告,以便更容易地部署资源来遏制和监控 暴发,这通常包括派遣受影响的鸡群和处理死鸟。该州敦促生产者和后院鸡群所有者加强生物安全措施,以防止进一步传播。

analysis_zh.event: 在爱荷华州萨克县的商业火鸡群中检测到 高致病性禽流感 (HPAI),这是近一年来首次发现此类 暴发。爱荷华州农业和土地管理部报告了此案。

NOTE: All AFD blogs are written by a human - any mistakes are solely mine. Thursday, October 29, 2026 Preprint: Why Americans Choose Raw Milk: Evidence from a National Quantitative Survey #19,391 With reports of H5N1 infected dairy herds increasing again (see Washington State: H5N1 Detections in Cattle Triple (n=27) - 2nd County (Benton) Affected), we are seeing an uptick in warnings from health departments about the dangers of consuming raw milk. The King County, WA Dept. of Public Health unambiguously warns: Raw (unpasteurized) milk and raw milk products Consuming raw milk and raw milk products can pose health risks. Raw milk and A(H5N1) virus The CDC recommends against consuming raw milk contaminated with live A(H5N1) virus as a way to develop antibodies against A(H5N1) virus to protect against future disease. Consuming raw milk could make you sick. Why is raw milk unsafe? Raw milk is milk from animals, typically cows and goats, which has not been pasteurized. Pasteurization is a process of heating raw milk to kill germs from the animal that are present in the raw milk. Some people believe that raw milk is more nutritious than pasteurized milk; however, the major nutrients in milk are not affected by pasteurization. Raw milk and raw milk products, such as cream, cheese and yogurt can be contaminated with harmful bacteria and cause serious infections. People with weakened immune systems, young children, the elderly, and pregnant women are at increased risk for severe infections from raw milk and milk products. It is especially important that young children, elderly persons, and persons with weakened immune systems consume only pasteurized milk and milk products. Read the label! In Washington state, it is legal to sell raw milk but raw milk products must be clearly labeled. In the fall of 2024, we saw similar warnings after a number of household pets were infected with H5N1, some presumably from exposure to raw milk and/or raw pet food (see LA County Issues Another Raw Milk Warning). Despite ample evidence of its dangers, most states allow its sale from farms or co-ops, and some states - like Washington - allow it to be sold in grocery stores alongside pasteurized milk. State Laws on sale of raw milk - Credit CDC A 2022 study published in the Journal of Food Protection found that: Results show that 4.4% of U.S. adults reported consuming raw milk at least once in the past year, with 1.6% reporting frequent consumption of raw milk (once per month or more often) and 1.0% reporting consumption once per week or more often. Today we have a new preprint - published Oct 28th - which suggests Americans' consumption of raw milk may be even higher than previously reported. It is based on a survey of 1,075 eligible US adults through an online panel in February of 2025, and it reports roughly 15% of US adults consumed raw milk in the preceding six months. While it is possible that pro-raw-milk enthusiasts were more likely to respond to this survey, recruitment was done through Qualtrics Research Services - using demographic quotas - not an openly advertised public poll. I've posted the abstract below, but those wishing a deeper dive will want to follow the link to read the preprint in its entirety. Why Americans Choose Raw Milk: Evidence from a National Quantitative Survey Sophia Ruser, Cristina Rojo, Katherine J Koebel, Calvin Slaughter, Ece Bulut, Renata Ivanek doi: https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.10.26.26366487 This article is a preprint and has not been certified by peer review Preview PDF Abstract Raw milk consumption is a controllable source of foodborne pathogen exposure in the United States (US), yet existing national estimates of raw milk consumption behaviors are outdated and do not capture emerging factors such as consumers' trusted information sources, sociopolitical influences, and at-home risk mitigation behaviors. We conducted a nationally representative cross-sectional survey of n=1078 US adults to estimate the prevalence of raw milk consumption and at-home thermal treatment practices and identify predictors of these behaviors. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to evaluate predictors of raw milk consumption and thermal treatment behavior using adjusted odds ratios (aORs). Among 1,075 eligible respondents, 15% consumed raw milk in the last six months, including 5% exclusively and 10% in addition to pasteurized milk. In multivariable analysis, raw milk consumption was independently associated with younger age, cohabitation with high-risk individuals for foodborne infections (including children less than or equal to five years of age, and elderly, pregnant or immunocompromised individuals) who had consumed raw milk, and perceptions of raw milk taste and safety. Adults aged greater than or equal to 55 years had lower odds of consumption than those aged 18-24 years (aOR, 0.05; 95% CI, 0.02-0.15), while those living with a high-risk household member who consumed raw milk had higher odds of consumption (aOR, 4.39; 95% CI, 2.69-7.22). Perceiving raw milk to have higher risk of causing illness was associated with lower odds of raw milk consumption (aOR: 0.32, 95% CI: 0.17-0.62) compared to believing the risk to be equal across milk types, and thermal treatment was reported by 38% of exclusive raw milk consumers (n=58) and 47% of consumers of both milk types (n=106). Raw milk consumption in the US appears to be substantially more common than previously reported and shaped by factors such as taste, safety, and household raw milk consumption among high-risk individuals for foodborne infections. The proportion of raw milk consumers already practicing at-home thermal treatment suggests a potential opportunity for risk mitigation. While all of this is self-reported and unverified information, it appears that among the respondents to this poll that high-risk groups (young children, elderly persons, and persons with weakened immune systems) are often cited as household consumers of raw milk. 10.0% reported a child aged five or younger who had consumed it. 9.1% reported an adult aged 65 or older. 3.2% reported an immunocompromised person. 2.1% reported a pregnant person. One potential bright spot, however, is the reported practice of heating or steaming raw milk (44% reported doing so > 50% of the time). Whether their heating temperatures and times were sufficient to kill pathogens is unknown. Since we've seen multiple instances where H5N1 contaminated raw milk has reached store shelves (see California: CDFA Announces Another Recall of H5 Contaminated Raw Milk), the risks - while low - are genuine. But whether any of this will dissuade those currently inclined to consume raw milk - after decades of near universal public health advice to the contrary - remains to be seen. Wednesday, October 28, 2026 WHO: Fatal H1N1v Infection In Brazil #19,390 Overnight the World Health Organization published its latest Influenza at the human-animal interface summary and assessment, 7 October 2026, which describes one previously reported H5N1 case from Cambodia, 4 recent H9N2 cases reported from Mainland China, and one fatal H1N1v case from Brazil. The H1N1v case is unusual in that the adult female patient - who had (unspecified) pre-existing chronic conditions - died after a month-long hospitalization. Of note: Her husband and three adult children also reported flu-like symptoms - were treated for a `viral infection' - but were never tested. According to the timeline provided by this report, the hospitalized case was only identified as having a novel flu (H1N1v) a week after her death. As a result, epidemiological investigation wasn't begun until September 5th, roughly 7 weeks after she (and her family) first fell ill. First, the WHO report, after which I'll return with more. Swine influenza viruses in humans Influenza A(H1N1)v, Brazil On 30 September 2026, Brazil notified PAHO/WHO of a laboratory-confirmed human infection with an influenza A(H1N1)v virus in an adult woman, with pre-existing chronic conditions, residing in the state of Santa Catarina. She developed symptoms of influenza-like illness on 16 July 2026 and sought medical attention on 20 July. Her husband and three adult children, who live in the same household,also experienced symptoms of an influenza-like illness; at that time, all were diagnosed, based solely on clinical examination, with a viral infection and received treatment. The woman, however, did not recover. On 27 July, the patient was hospitalized due to worsening respiratory symptoms. She received treatment, including the antiviral oseltamivir, and required intensive care, including ventilatory support. Despite intensive care, the patient passed away on 28 August. A nasopharyngeal sample, collected on 29 July, tested positive for influenza A on 30 July and was subsequently subtyped as influenza A(H1N1) on 31 July. The sample was sent to the reference laboratory for respiratory viruses at the Oswaldo Cruz Institute (IOC/Fiocruz) in Rio de Janeiro for further characterization. On 4 September, genomic analysis identified an influenza A(H1N1)v virus. According to information gathered during an epidemiological investigation conducted by municipal and state teams between 5 and 9 September, the patient had no history of travel or direct contact with swine. However, a possible indirect exposure to swine was identified through a neighbour who raises these animals for personal consumption. Since 2015, twelve cases of human infection with swine-origin virus variants, including this one, have been detected within Brazil’s respiratory virus surveillance workflow. This chronology illustrates just how difficult it can be to detect a novel virus, even when the patient is hospitalized with severe influenza. A few recent examples include: In November of 2025, Washington State reported the first known human infection with avian H5N5; a diagnosis that was delayed - according to an MMWR report - by `early and repeated negative influenza test results from upper respiratory swab specimens'. In 2024, a Missouri patient was hospitalized with influenza A, and released, before being notified they had H5N1 (see Missouri DHSS: Human H5 bird flu case confirmed in Missouri). Also in 2024, Australia treated a child with recent travel from India for severe flu, which resulted in respiratory failure. The child fell ill (in India) in late February, was hospitalized in Melbourne in early March, and was released after > 2 weeks. While respiratory samples were taken in early March, they weren't identified as H5N1 positive until mid-May. Complicating matters, most people experiencing mild or moderate flu symptoms are unlikely to seek medical care, and even when they do, they are often treated for a `viral illness' and never tested. We've seen past studies (see here, here, and here) suggesting that as few as 1 in 100 cases are identified in the community. In early 2025, the CDC issued a HAN: Accelerated Subtyping of Influenza A in Hospitalized Patients, requesting that all hospitalized patients with suspected influenza be subtyped within 24 hours. More recently, we saw Washington State: Updated guidance for novel influenza screening and influenza subtyping, which emphasized the importance of identifying those with acute respiratory illness (ARI) and specific epidemiologic risk factors. The reality is, it takes a certain degree of luck to detect sporadic novel flu infections in the community. While better screening methods could improve detection rates, many mild and moderate infections will still likely fly beneath our radar. A reminder than anything we say about the current threat from H5N1, swine flu variants, MERS-CoV, or any other pandemic threat must carry an implied asterisk. A disclaimer that says, ` * based on available, and likely incomplete, information. . . '. Tuesday, October 27, 2026 Washington State: H5N1 Detections in Cattle Triple (n=27) - 2nd County (Benton) Affected #18,389 While it hasn't shown up yet on the USDA's H5N1 in Livestock dashboard, the number of dairy herds in Washington State infected with HPAI has jumped from 9 late last week, to 27, with a second county (Benton) now reporting an infected herd. Less than 3 weeks ago (Oct 8th) the USDA/APHIS announced the first detection of H5N1 in dairy cattle in Washington State, which was followed a week later by the first (reportedly mild) human H5N1 infection reported in the U.S. in 2026 (see Washington State Confirms Human Avian Flu Infection). Other than the (above) update to the Washington State Dept. Agriculture dashboard, I have found no other public announcement of this jump in detections. Yesterday, the WSDA did publish a statement on the detection of H5N1 in a second county, which also states: Media note: WSDA will issue a news release for each new county with confirmed HPAI in cattle. Subsequent detections in previously announced counties will be posted online. Excerpts from yesterday's announcement follow: WSDA confirms HPAI in dairy herd in Benton County OLYMPIA – Oct. 26, 2026 – Washington State Department of Agriculture (WSDA) has confirmed a detection of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 in a Benton County dairy herd. The virus was detected by the Washington Animal Disease Diagnostic Laboratory (WADDL) through routine surveillance, and the finding was confirmed by the USDA National Veterinary Services Laboratories (NVSL). The dairy herd is under quarantine and has employed strict biosecurity measures. Veterinarians are working to treat sick cows. Pasteurized milk products remain safe for consumers, and milk supply shortages are not expected. WSDA urges dairy farmers statewide to report any clinical signs of illness to their veterinarian, including: Changes in milk appearance (thicker, often yellowish to brown) Decreased milk production Decline in feed intake Fever Respiratory symptoms Changes in manure Steep drop in rumination and rumen motility If you notice any of these signs, isolate affected animals and contact your veterinarian and WSDA at 360-902-1878 or ahealth@agr.wa.gov. Most cattle affected by HPAI recover with supportive care with full herd recovery typically taking 4-6 weeks. “Seeing the virus move to another county is disappointing but our dairy farmers are working hard to implement their biosecurity plans, share lessons learned and help each other get through this,” said Washington State Veterinarian Amber Itle, VMD, MS. "This isn’t new for the country, but it is new for Washington. I’ve been in awe of how hard our veterinarians and dairy farmers work together every day to keep their cows healthy, keep their workers safe and keep operating despite all the uncertainty this virus brings with it. This detection was through routine surveillance enabling us to detect the virus before cows got sick. We hope this will help us to implement measures on farm to prevent transmission within or between other dairy or poultry facilities.” HPAI can spread between dairy cattle through infected animals and contaminated milk, equipment, vehicles, clothing, footwear and other materials or people that move between farms. Wild birds can also carry HPAI, but they are not considered the primary source of spread of the virus that affects dairy herds. Poultry are also highly susceptible to HPAI. Other states have reported infections in commercial and backyard poultry flocks near dairy farms affected by H5N1. Poultry owners, including those who keep backyard flocks, should remain vigilant for signs of illness and practice strong biosecurity to help reduce the risk of infection. (Continue . . .) According the WSDA, there are nearly 400 dairy farms in Washington State, which suggests that over the past 3 weeks roughly 7% of their dairy herds have tested positive for H5N1. Dairy product safety Pasteurization inactivates viruses and bacteria in milk, including HPAI virus, helping ensure the safety of the dairy supply. Infected cows can shed the virus in their milk, making raw milk and other raw dairy products unsafe for consumption. Avoid raw dairy product consumption, and do not allow your pets to consume raw milk or other dairy products, or raw foods such as raw meat. While the State of Washington posted the above warning on October 8th, Washington allows the sale of raw milk in grocery stores, natural food markets, food co-ops, and direct-to-consumer farm stores. Hopefully, the public is taking these risks seriously. ECDC & CDC Updates On Ebola Multi-country outbreak 2026 Credit CDC #19,388 With the number of confirmed cases nearing 10,000, the Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak in central Africa - which was first announced in mid-May in the DRC - is now the second largest in history, and shows no sign of stopping. Credit CDC This outbreak has spilled over into neighboring countries, and an imported case was recently reported in Nigeria (see ECDC Threat assessment brief – Importation of Ebola disease cases caused by Bundibugyo virus to Kenya and Nigeria). While sporadic exported cases are always possible, the public health risks outside of the DRC and surrounding areas is considered low. Yesterday the CDC (link) and the ECDC (link) both posted updated outbreak reports. Excerpts from both follow: Ebola disease: Multi-country outbreak 2026 This page is updated regularly. It was last updated on 26 October at 16:30. An outbreak of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus has been ongoing in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) since May 2026. Cases were also reported in Kenya and Nigeria in October 2026 and have been reported in Uganda, where the outbreak has ended. Key facts On 20 October 2026, an Ebola case was reported in Nigeria. The individual, who had travel history to Uganda, developed symptoms on 7 October, sought medical care on 11 October, and tested positive on 20…

Perceiving raw milk to have higher risk of causing illness was associated with lower odds of raw milk consumption (aOR: 0.32, 95% CI: 0.17-0.62) compared to believing the risk to be equal across milk types, and thermal treatment was reported by 38% of exclusive raw milk consumers (n=58) and 47% of consumers of both milk types (n=106). Raw milk consumption in the US appears to be substantially more common than previously reported and shaped by factors such as taste, safety, and household raw milk consumption among high-risk individuals for foodborne infections. The proportion of raw milk consumers already practicing at-home thermal treatment suggests a potential opportunity for risk mitigation. While all of this is self-reported and unverified information, it appears that among the respondents to this poll that high-risk groups (young children, elderly persons, and persons with weakened immune systems) are often cited as household consumers of raw milk. 10.0% reported a child aged five or younger who had consumed it. 9.1% reported an adult aged 65 or older. 3.2% reported an immunocompromised person. 2.1% reported a pregnant person. One potential bright spot, however, is the reported practice of heating or steaming raw milk (44% reported doing so > 50% of the time). Whether their heating temperatures and times were sufficient to kill pathogens is unknown. Since we've seen multiple instances where H5N1 contaminated raw milk has reached store shelves (see California: CDFA Announces Another Recall of H5 Contaminated Raw Milk), the risks - while low - are genuine. But whether any of this will dissuade those currently inclined to consume raw milk - after decades of near universal public health advice to the contrary - remains to be seen. Wednesday, October 28, 2026 WHO: Fatal H1N1v Infection In Brazil #19,390 Overnight the World Health Organization published its latest Influenza at the human-animal interface summary and assessment, 7 October 2026, which describes one previously reported H5N1 case from Cambodia, 4 recent H9N2 cases reported from Mainland China, and one fatal H1N1v case from Brazil. The H1N1v case is unusual in that the adult female patient - who had (unspecified) pre-existing chronic conditions - died after a month-long hospitalization. Of note: Her husband and three adult children also reported flu-like symptoms - were treated for a `viral infection' - but were never tested. According to the timeline provided by this report, the hospitalized case was only identified as having a novel flu (H1N1v) a week after her death. As a result, epidemiological investigation wasn't begun until September 5th, roughly 7 weeks after she (and her family) first fell ill. First, the WHO report, after which I'll return with more. Swine influenza viruses in humans Influenza A(H1N1)v, Brazil On 30 September 2026, Brazil notified PAHO/WHO of a laboratory-confirmed human infection with an influenza A(H1N1)v virus in an adult woman, with pre-existing chronic conditions, residing in the state of Santa Catarina. She developed symptoms of influenza-like illness on 16 July 2026 and sought medical attention on 20 July. Her husband and three adult children, who live in the same household,also experienced symptoms of an influenza-like illness; at that time, all were diagnosed, based solely on clinical examination, with a viral infection and received treatment. The woman, however, did not recover. On 27 July, the patient was hospitalized due to worsening respiratory symptoms. She received treatment, including the antiviral oseltamivir, and required intensive care, including ventilatory support. Despite intensive care, the patient passed away on 28 August. A nasopharyngeal sample, collected on 29 July, tested positive for influenza A on 30 July and was subsequently subtyped as influenza A(H1N1) on 31 July. The sample was sent to the reference laboratory for respiratory viruses at the Oswaldo Cruz Institute (IOC/Fiocruz) in Rio de Janeiro for further characterization. On 4 September, genomic analysis identified an influenza A(H1N1)v virus. According to information gathered during an epidemiological investigation conducted by municipal and state teams between 5 and 9 September, the patient had no history of travel or direct contact with swine. However, a possible indirect exposure to swine was identified through a neighbour who raises these animals for personal consumption. Since 2015, twelve cases of human infection with swine-origin virus variants, including this one, have been detected within Brazil’s respiratory virus surveillance workflow. This chronology illustrates just how difficult it can be to detect a novel virus, even when the patient is hospitalized with severe influenza. A few recent examples include: In November of 2025, Washington State reported the first known human infection with avian H5N5; a diagnosis that was delayed - according to an MMWR report - by `early and repeated negative influenza test results from upper respiratory swab specimens'. In 2024, a Missouri patient was hospitalized with influenza A, and released, before being notified they had H5N1 (see Missouri DHSS: Human H5 bird flu case confirmed in Missouri). Also in 2024, Australia treated a child with recent travel from India for severe flu, which resulted in respiratory failure. The child fell ill (in India) in late February, was hospitalized in Melbourne in early March, and was released after > 2 weeks. While respiratory samples were taken in early March, they weren't identified as H5N1 positive until mid-May. Complicating matters, most people experiencing mild or moderate flu symptoms are unlikely to seek medical care, and even when they do, they are often treated for a `viral illness' and never tested. We've seen past studies (see here, here, and here) suggesting that as few as 1 in 100 cases are identified in the community. In early 2025, the CDC issued a HAN: Accelerated Subtyping of Influenza A in Hospitalized Patients, requesting that all hospitalized patients with suspected influenza be subtyped within 24 hours. More recently, we saw Washington State: Updated guidance for novel influenza screening and influenza subtyping, which emphasized the importance of identifying those with acute respiratory illness (ARI) and specific epidemiologic risk factors. The reality is, it takes a certain degree of luck to detect sporadic novel flu infections in the community. While better screening methods could improve detection rates, many mild and moderate infections will still likely fly beneath our radar. A reminder than anything we say about the current threat from H5N1, swine flu variants, MERS-CoV, or any other pandemic threat must carry an implied asterisk. A disclaimer that says, ` * based on available, and likely incomplete, information. . . '. Tuesday, October 27, 2026 Washington State: H5N1 Detections in Cattle Triple (n=27) - 2nd County (Benton) Affected #18,389 While it hasn't shown up yet on the USDA's H5N1 in Livestock dashboard, the number of dairy herds in Washington State infected with HPAI has jumped from 9 late last week, to 27, with a second county (Benton) now reporting an infected herd. Less than 3 weeks ago (Oct 8th) the USDA/APHIS announced the first detection of H5N1 in dairy cattle in Washington State, which was followed a week later by the first (reportedly mild) human H5N1 infection reported in the U.S. in 2026 (see Washington State Confirms Human Avian Flu Infection). Other than the (above) update to the Washington State Dept. Agriculture dashboard, I have found no other public announcement of this jump in detections. Yesterday, the WSDA did publish a statement on the detection of H5N1 in a second county, which also states: Media note: WSDA will issue a news release for each new county with confirmed HPAI in cattle. Subsequent detections in previously announced counties will be posted online. Excerpts from yesterday's announcement follow: WSDA confirms HPAI in dairy herd in Benton County OLYMPIA – Oct. 26, 2026 – Washington State Department of Agriculture (WSDA) has confirmed a detection of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 in a Benton County dairy herd. The virus was detected by the Washington Animal Disease Diagnostic Laboratory (WADDL) through routine surveillance, and the finding was confirmed by the USDA National Veterinary Services Laboratories (NVSL). The dairy herd is under quarantine and has employed strict biosecurity measures. Veterinarians are working to treat sick cows. Pasteurized milk products remain safe for consumers, and milk supply shortages are not expected. WSDA urges dairy farmers statewide to report any clinical signs of illness to their veterinarian, including: Changes in milk appearance (thicker, often yellowish to brown) Decreased milk production Decline in feed intake Fever Respiratory symptoms Changes in manure Steep drop in rumination and rumen motility If you notice any of these signs, isolate affected animals and contact your veterinarian and WSDA at 360-902-1878 or ahealth@agr.wa.gov. Most cattle affected by HPAI recover with supportive care with full herd recovery typically taking 4-6 weeks. “Seeing the virus move to another county is disappointing but our dairy farmers are working hard to implement their biosecurity plans, share lessons learned and help each other get through this,” said Washington State Veterinarian Amber Itle, VMD, MS. "This isn’t new for the country, but it is new for Washington. I’ve been in awe of how hard our veterinarians and dairy farmers work together every day to keep their cows healthy, keep their workers safe and keep operating despite all the uncertainty this virus brings with it. This detection was through routine surveillance enabling us to detect the virus before cows got sick. We hope this will help us to implement measures on farm to prevent transmission within or between other dairy or poultry facilities.” HPAI can spread between dairy cattle through infected animals and contaminated milk, equipment, vehicles, clothing, footwear and other materials or people that move between farms. Wild birds can also carry HPAI, but they are not considered the primary source of spread of the virus that affects dairy herds. Poultry are also highly susceptible to HPAI. Other states have reported infections in commercial and backyard poultry flocks near dairy farms affected by H5N1. Poultry owners, including those who keep backyard flocks, should remain vigilant for signs of illness and practice strong biosecurity to help reduce the risk of infection. (Continue . . .) According the WSDA, there are nearly 400 dairy farms in Washington State, which suggests that over the past 3 weeks roughly 7% of their dairy herds have tested positive for H5N1. Dairy product safety Pasteurization inactivates viruses and bacteria in milk, including HPAI virus, helping ensure the safety of the dairy supply. Infected cows can shed the virus in their milk, making raw milk and other raw dairy products unsafe for consumption. Avoid raw dairy product consumption, and do not allow your pets to consume raw milk or other dairy products, or raw foods such as raw meat. While the State of Washington posted the above warning on October 8th, Washington allows the sale of raw milk in grocery stores, natural food markets, food co-ops, and direct-to-consumer farm stores. Hopefully, the public is taking these risks seriously. news.content_zh: 《禽流感日记》的报告强调了华盛顿州牛中 H5N1 病毒检出率的上升,截至 2026 年 10 月 29 日报告了 27 例病例,使本顿县成为第二个受影响地区。它还引用了 2026 年 10 月 28 日发表的一项预印本研究,该研究表明 15% 的美国成年人在过去六个月内食用了生牛奶,其中幼儿、老年人和免疫功能低下者等高风险群体被列为家庭消费者。华盛顿州金县公共卫生部警告不要食用生奶,因为存在潜在的健康风险,而疾病预防控制中心则建议不要食用受 A(H5N1) 病毒污染的生奶。该研究于 2025 年 2 月进行,属于自我报告且未经证实,研究指出 44% 的原奶消费者实行家庭热饮 治疗。此外,该报告还提到巴西发生了致命的 H1N1v 感染,该感染是在患者死亡一周后发现的,强调了人畜共患流感 传播 的持续风险。研究结果强调,需要对原奶消费和流感预防继续保持警惕并提供公共卫生指导。

Privacy Policy Accept Deny Non-Essential Storage Preferences Subscribe Sign In Donate Manage Subscription Update Profile Sign Out Donate Today's Paper Local News 2026 Voter Guide Simmons Bank Championship High School Football Health Beat Lab Best of the Best Obits Funded Stories Puzzles Newsletters Legal Notices Opinion Archives Bird flu case reported in Baxter County backyard flock October 28, 2026 by ARKANSAS DEMOCRAT-GAZETTE 0 Comments 0 Comments × If the highly pathogenic avian influenza virus fully adapts to humans, covid-19 will look like a small cold compared to what this virus could cause, according to Guillermo Tellez-Isaias, the chairman of the International Avian Influenza and One Health Emerging Issues Summit. (Special to The Commercial/University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture) Let us read it for you. Listen now. Your browser does not support the audio element. Arkansas' first case of highly pathogenic avian influenza this season was reported Tuesday by the state Department of Agriculture in a backyard domestic poultry flock in eastern Baxter County. "While this is currently the only detection in Arkansas, increasing detections in other states reinforce the importance of continued prevention and monitoring," the department said in a news release. The avian influenza, or bird flu, is a highly contagious virus that affects domestic and wild birds. It has caused sudden death or severe illness in poultry and can lead to economic losses in the state's poultry industry. Poultry production in Arkansas is valued at more than $6.7 billion annually, the department said. The virus spreads through contact with infected birds, contaminated equipment, or materials. "Under Arkansas state rule, any suspected or confirmed case of avian influenza must be reported immediately to the department," the news release said. "State regulations authorize the department to quarantine infected premises, restrict poultry movement within designated control zones, and require depopulation and disinfection when necessary to prevent further spread." Poultry owners should follow safety practices that include washing hands and shoes before and after contact with birds, limiting exposure to wild birds, restricting visitors to poultry areas, and quarantining new birds for at least two weeks. Poultry owners can also report any unusual illness or sudden deaths in their flocks to the Arkansas Department of Agriculture at (501) 823-1746. × You're one step away from the full story. (Special to The Commercial/University of Arkansas System Division of Agriculture) Let us read it for you. Listen now. Your browser does not support the audio element. Arkansas' first case of highly pathogenic avian influenza this season was reported Tuesday by the state Department of Agriculture in a backyard domestic poultry flock in eastern Baxter County. "While this is currently the only detection in Arkansas, increasing detections in other states reinforce the importance of continued prevention and monitoring," the department said in a news release. The avian influenza, or bird flu, is a highly contagious virus that affects domestic and wild birds. It has caused sudden death or severe illness in poultry and can lead to economic losses in the state's poultry industry. Poultry production in Arkansas is valued at more than $6.7 billion annually, the department said. The virus spreads through contact with infected birds, contaminated equipment, or materials. "Under Arkansas state rule, any suspected or confirmed case of avian influenza must be reported immediately to the department," the news release said. "State regulations authorize the department to quarantine infected premises, restrict poultry movement within designated control zones, and require depopulation and disinfection when necessary to prevent further spread." Poultry owners should follow safety practices that include washing hands and shoes before and after contact with birds, limiting exposure to wild birds, restricting visitors to poultry areas, and quarantining new birds for at least two weeks. Poultry owners can also report any unusual illness or sudden deaths in their flocks to the Arkansas Department of Agriculture at (501) 823-1746. × You're one step away from the full story. They also highlight the potential impact that the decline in vultures could have on ecosystems and human wellbeing. To address this situation, they propose five courses of action: to monitor vulture populations, implement vaccination campaigns, manage the carrion, establish protocols for handling vultures, and promote local action plans. Vultures are one of the most threatened group of birds in the world. Currently, at least 16 of the 23 species of vulture are of conservation concern, largely as a result of poisoning and other threats due to human activity. However, “they provide us with one of the most important ecosystem services for human wellbeing: they feed on decomposing animal carcasses, that harbour pathogens. It has been proven that scavengers help prevent or reduce the spread of pathogens. That is, they prevent disease-causing microorganisms from continuing to spread”, explains Jon Morant, researcher at the EHU-University of the Basque Country. The avian flu virus (H5N1), which caused the panzootic —the equivalent of a pandemic in animals—, is highly contagious and could lead to the collapse of vulture populations, which are already in decline. In fact, it has been confirmed that the virus has spread widely in certain areas of the world that are critical for vultures, which has had serious consequences. For example, thousands of American black vultures (Coragyps atratus) and Turkey vultures (Cathartes aura) have died in the United States and South America. The virus has also had a significant impact on the Bearded vulture (Gypaetus barbatus) in Europe and the California condor (Gymnogyps californianus) and Andean condor (Vultur gryphus) in America. It should be noted that the California condor is critically endangered and that its wild population fell by 6% in just six weeks. To warn of this threat and to establish courses of action to address the problem, Jon Morant, researcher at the Department of Zoology and Animal Cell Biology of the EHU, published a letter in the journal Conservation Biology, together with several researchers at the Mediterranean Institute for Advanced Studies (IMEDEA, Mallorca) and the Institute for Research in Biodiversity and Environment (INIBIOMA, Argentina). “We wanted to alert the research community and those responsible for conservation so that they could establish coordinated actions”, explains Morant. A paradox In general, “vultures are social animals and gather together at the feeding stations; that is, places where the risk of contagion is high. Moreover, they could contract the H5N1 virus if they consume infected animal carcasses. As scavengers, vultures are resistant to many bacteria and pathogens. However, this is not enough to protect them from the H5N1 virus”, explains Morant. The virus has a high fatality rate in both domestic and wild animals. Avian influenza does not exclusively affect birds: it has been documented that more than 48 species of mammal around the world have been infected. “The greater the number of infected carcasses, the greater the risk of contagion for the vultures. Since these carcasses can become sources of infection, a paradox arises: as more vultures die, the capacity to eliminate the carrion reduces, the pathogens spread and contagion increases”, explains the researcher. Five courses of action Researchers who sign the letter call on conservationists and managers to adopt a holistic and multi-dimensional approach to reducing the threat posed to vultures by the H5N1 virus. Firstly, they consider it urgent to monitor vulture populations. “In the Basque Country, the Griffon vulture population is in a healthy condition, but the Egyptian vulture is a more sensitive. We need to pay particular attention to migratory species”, explains Morant. Secondly, they propose implementing vaccination campaigns when populations are at serious risk and where logistical conditions permit. “In the United States, in the case of the California condor, the research community has implemented a vaccination campaign in response to the high risk of the species becoming extinct”, he added. The third course of action focuses on feeding stations for scavenger birds. “It is important that they are fed with non-contaminated carcasses.” The fourth course of action is aimed at researchers: “They must comply strictly with biosecurity protocols (use gloves, masks and protective equipment), especially when working with small populations or with threatened species.” Finally, they recommend developing and promoting action plans adapted to each context, since the countries where the vultures live have different socio-economic situations and highly diverse governance models. The signatories of the letter are concerned about the problem and hope that, while the letter remains open, researchers and conservation managers will start to take action. “We propose using the letter as guide. To tackle this dangerous epidemiological situation, it is urgent to develop coordinated cross-border plans and to integrate these actions into shared governance structures”, concludes Morant. Additional information In addition to Jon Morant from the EHU, Andrea Santangeli (IMEDEA), Pablo Plaza (INIBIOMA) and Sergio A. Lambertucci (INIBIOMA) also signed the card. Morant is a lecturer and researcher at the Álava Campus of the EHU, though he is currently undertaking a stay at the UCD School of Biology and Environmental Science, Dublin, as part of a Basque Government postdoctoral programme. They also highlight the potential impact that the decline in vultures could have on ecosystems and human wellbeing. To address this situation, they propose five courses of action: to monitor vulture populations, implement vaccination campaigns, manage the carrion, establish protocols for handling vultures, and promote local action plans. Vultures are one of the most threatened group of birds in the world. Currently, at least 16 of the 23 species of vulture are of conservation concern, largely as a result of poisoning and other threats due to human activity. However, “they provide us with one of the most important ecosystem services for human wellbeing: they feed on decomposing animal carcasses, that harbour pathogens. It has been proven that scavengers help prevent or reduce the spread of pathogens. That is, they prevent disease-causing microorganisms from continuing to spread”, explains Jon Morant, researcher at the EHU-University of the Basque Country. The avian flu virus (H5N1), which caused the panzootic —the equivalent of a pandemic in animals—, is highly contagious and could lead to the collapse of vulture populations, which are already in decline. In fact, it has been confirmed that the virus has spread widely in certain areas of the world that are critical for vultures, which has had serious consequences. For example, thousands of American black vultures (Coragyps atratus) and Turkey vultures (Cathartes aura) have died in the United States and South America. The virus has also had a significant impact on the Bearded vulture (Gypaetus barbatus) in Europe and the California condor (Gymnogyps californianus) and Andean condor (Vultur gryphus) in America. It should be noted that the California condor is critically endangered and that its wild population fell by 6% in just six weeks. To warn of this threat and to establish courses of action to address the problem, Jon Morant, researcher at the Department of Zoology and Animal Cell Biology of the EHU, published a letter in the journal Conservation Biology, together with several researchers at the Mediterranean Institute for Advanced Studies (IMEDEA, Mallorca) and the Institute for Research in Biodiversity and Environment (INIBIOMA, Argentina). “We wanted to alert the research community and those responsible for conservation so that they could establish coordinated actions”, explains Morant. A paradox In general, “vultures are social animals and gather together at the feeding stations; that is, places where the risk of contagion is high. Moreover, they could contract the H5N1 virus if they consume infected animal carcasses. As scavengers, vultures are resistant to many bacteria and pathogens. However, this is not enough to protect them from the H5N1 virus”, explains Morant. The virus has a high fatality rate in both domestic and wild animals. Avian influenza does not exclusively affect birds: it has been documented that more than 48 species of mammal around the world have been infected. “The greater the number of infected carcasses, the greater the risk of contagion for the vultures. Since these carcasses can become sources of infection, a paradox arises: as more vultures die, the capacity to eliminate the carrion reduces, the pathogens spread and contagion increases”, explains the researcher. Five courses of action Researchers who sign the letter call on conservationists and managers to adopt a holistic and multi-dimensional approach to reducing the threat posed to vultures by the H5N1 virus. Firstly, they consider it urgent to monitor vulture populations. “In the Basque Country, the Griffon vulture population is in a healthy condition, but the Egyptian vulture is a more sensitive. We need to pay particular attention to migratory species”, explains Morant. Secondly, they propose implementing vaccination campaigns when populations are at serious risk and where logistical conditions permit. “In the United States, in the case of the California condor, the research community has implemented a vaccination campaign in response to the high risk of the species becoming extinct”, he added. The third course of action focuses on feeding stations for scavenger birds. “It is important that they are fed with non-contaminated carcasses.” The fourth course of action is aimed at researchers: “They must comply strictly with biosecurity protocols (use gloves, masks and protective equipment), especially when working with small populations or with threatened species.” Finally, they recommend developing and promoting action plans adapted to each context, since the countries where the vultures live have different socio-economic situations and highly diverse governance models. The signatories of the letter are concerned about the problem and hope that, while the letter remains open, researchers and conservation managers will start to take action. “We propose using the letter as guide. To tackle this dangerous epidemiological situation, it is urgent to develop coordinated cross-border plans and to integrate these actions into shared governance structures”, concludes Morant. Additional information In addition to Jon Morant from the EHU, Andrea Santangeli (IMEDEA), Pablo Plaza (INIBIOMA) and Sergio A. Lambertucci (INIBIOMA) also signed the card. Morant is a lecturer and researcher at the Álava Campus of the EHU, though he is currently undertaking a stay at the UCD School of Biology and Environmental Science, Dublin, as part of a Basque Government postdoctoral programme. analysis.brief_en: A study led by Jon Morant from the EHU-University of the Basque Country, along with researchers from IMEDEA and INIBIOMA, highlights the growing threat of avian influenza, specifically H5N1, to vulture populations worldwide. The virus has caused widespread mortality in vulture species, particularly in the United States and South America, where thousands of American black vultures and Turkey vultures have died. The decline in vulture numbers is exacerbated by human activities, such as poisoning, and the virus's high fatality rate in both domestic and wild animals. Vultures, as scavengers, play a crucial role in preventing the spread of pathogens, but their susceptibility to H5N1 creates a paradox: as more vultures die, the capacity to remove infected carcasses diminishes, increasing the risk of pathogen spread. The researchers propose five measures, including population monitoring, vaccination campaigns, managing feeding stations with non-contaminated carcasses, strict biosecurity protocols, and context-specific action plans, to mitigate the threat. These actions are intended to be coordinated across borders and integrated into shared governance structures to protect vultures and maintain ecosystem balance.
