The decline in vulture numbers is exacerbated by human activities, such as poisoning, and the virus's high fatality rate in both domestic and wild animals. Vultures, as scavengers, play a crucial role in preventing the spread of pathogens, but their susceptibility to H5N1 creates a paradox: as more vultures die, the capacity to remove infected carcasses diminishes, increasing the risk of pathogen spread. The researchers propose five measures, including population monitoring, vaccination campaigns, managing feeding stations with non-contaminated carcasses, strict biosecurity protocols, and context-specific action plans, to mitigate the threat. These actions are intended to be coordinated across borders and integrated into shared governance structures to protect vultures and maintain ecosystem balance.

news.content_zh: 巴斯克地区 EHU 大学的乔恩·莫兰特 (Jon Morant) 与 IMEDEA 和 INIBIOMA 的研究人员领导的一项研究强调了 禽流感(特别是 H5N1)对全世界秃鹫种群的日益严重的威胁。该病毒已在秃鹫物种中造成广泛的死亡率,特别是在美国和南美洲,数千只美洲黑秃鹫和土耳其秃鹫死亡。中毒等人类活动以及病毒在家畜和野生动物中的高死亡率加剧了秃鹫数量的下降。秃鹫作为食腐动物,在防止病原体传播方面发挥着至关重要的作用,但它们对 H5N1 病毒的易感性造成了一个悖论:随着越来越多的秃鹫死亡,清除受感染尸体的能力就会减弱,从而增加了病原体传播的风险。研究人员提出了五项措施来减轻威胁,包括种群监测、疫苗接种 活动、管理未受污染尸体的饲养站、严格的生物安全协议和针对具体情况的行动计划。这些行动旨在跨境协调并纳入共享治理结构,以保护秃鹫并维持生态系统平衡。

analysis.time: The bird flu cases were confirmed on October 27, 2026, in eastern Baxter County, Arkansas, and the disaster proclamation was issued on October 28, 2026, by Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds.
analysis.location_and_population: The cases were reported in Sac County, Iowa, and eastern Baxter County, Arkansas, affecting commercial turkey flocks and backyard poultry flocks.
analysis.event: H5N1 bird flu was confirmed in a commercial turkey flock in Sac County, Iowa, and in a backyard poultry flock in eastern Baxter County, Arkansas. The Iowa governor issued a disaster proclamation to allocate state resources for tracking, containment, and cleanup.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak is part of the 2026–27 season, with Iowa reporting its eighth case in 2026. Officials stated that the detections pose no immediate public-health concern and poultry products remain safe to eat.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Officials in both states urged flock owners to strengthen biosecurity, monitor for illness or sudden deaths, and report suspected cases promptly. The virus is highly contagious, and authorities emphasized the need for biosecurity measures and keeping poultry indoors when possible.

analysis.brief_en: Bird flu cases, specifically H5N1, have been confirmed in both Iowa and Arkansas. In Iowa, the virus was detected in a commercial turkey flock in Sac County, prompting Governor Kim Reynolds to issue a disaster proclamation on October 28, 2026, to mobilize state resources for tracking, containment, and cleanup. Arkansas confirmed its first case of the 2026–27 season on October 27, 2026, in a backyard poultry flock in eastern Baxter County. Officials in both states have urged poultry owners to enhance biosecurity, monitor for signs of illness or sudden deaths, and report suspected cases immediately. While the outbreak is ongoing, Iowa officials have stated that the detections pose no immediate public health risk, and poultry products are considered safe for consumption. The virus is highly contagious, and authorities have emphasized the importance of keeping poultry indoors and implementing strict biosecurity protocols to prevent further spread.

(KATV) — The Arkansas Department of Agriculture has confirmed the first case of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) for the season. Department officials confirmed the virus in a backyard domestic poultry flock in eastern Baxter County on Oct. 27. While this is currently the only detection in Arkansas, increasing detections in other states reinforce the importance of continued prevention and monitoring," The department said in a release HPAI is a highly contagious virus that can cause sudden death or severe illness in both wild and domestic birds. Agriculture experts said the disease can spread easily through contact with infected birds, contaminated equipment or materials. It can also lead to major economic losses for producers and the state poultry industry, which is valued at $6.7 billion annually. You can reach the department by calling (501)823-1746. supplementary_news.content: An outbreak of highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza has been spreading uncontrolled for more than two months across a commercial mink fur farm south of Salt Lake City, triggering severe criticism from infectious disease specialists who warn that governmental inaction is creating a dangerous breeding ground for potential human viral adaptation. The outbreak, centered at C&T Fenn Farms near Payson in Utah County, represents the first documented detection of H5N1 bird flu in captive mink on American soil. Internal communications and veterinary records obtained through public records requests by the Animal Welfare Institute (AWI) and investigated by ProPublica reveal that the virus has killed thousands of animals, with the facility projecting a total mortality rate of approximately 80 percent. Yet, unlike federal protocols governing poultry and dairy operations, state and federal regulators have not depopulated the herd, enforced a legally binding quarantine, or conducted routine symptom surveillance among exposed farmhands. Flu researchers and biosecurity experts have described the administrative response as an alarming departure from global disease containment standards, warning that allowing the virus to circulate unhindered through dense mammal populations heightens the probability of genetic mutations capable of crossing into the human population. Why Scientists Consider Mink the 'Perfect Petri Dish' While the current H5N1 strain has infected dairy cattle across the country and led to sporadic human infections in farmworkers exposed to livestock, it has lacked the biological capability to transmit efficiently from person to person. Avian influenza viruses preferentially bind to alpha-2,3 sialic acid receptors predominantly found in the respiratory tracts of birds. Mink, however, represent a unique biological conduit: Human-Like Cellular Architecture: The upper respiratory tracts of mink feature an abundance of alpha-2,6 sialic acid receptors—the exact cellular gateway influenza viruses exploit to infect human nasal passages and throats. The upper respiratory tracts of mink feature an abundance of alpha-2,6 sialic acid receptors—the exact cellular gateway influenza viruses exploit to infect human nasal passages and throats. Aerosol Transmission Risks: Prior peer-reviewed research, including studies published in Nature Communications and Emerging Microbes & Infections, has demonstrated that mink can transmit respiratory viruses efficiently through aerosolized droplets when housed in close proximity. Prior peer-reviewed research, including studies published in Nature Communications and Emerging Microbes & Infections, has demonstrated that mink can transmit respiratory viruses efficiently through aerosolized droplets when housed in close proximity. The Reassortment Threat: Because mink are susceptible to both human seasonal flu and avian influenza, co-infection within a single host cell can trigger genetic reassortment—a process where two distinct viruses swap gene segments. With the 2026–2027 human flu season underway earlier than usual, scientists caution that coinfection could yield a novel, hybrid pandemic strain. Because mink are susceptible to both human seasonal flu and avian influenza, co-infection within a single host cell can trigger genetic reassortment—a process where two distinct viruses swap gene segments. With the 2026–2027 human flu season underway earlier than usual, scientists caution that coinfection could yield a novel, hybrid pandemic strain. The Dairy Connection: Genomic sequencing conducted by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) confirmed that the Utah mink were infected with the identical B3.13 genotype circulating in American dairy herds. Farm operators routinely feed raw livestock offal and unpasteurized slaughterhouse tissue to mink during summer months to accelerate pelt growth. "Mink to mink transmission is where the danger escalates," said Gail Hansen, a former state public health veterinarian and epidemiologist. "As long as it continues to go mink to mink, it becomes more and more likely that it could jump to a human." Regulatory Paralysis: No Cull, No Quarantine, and 'Verbal Holds' When avian influenza strikes commercial poultry, federal policy is absolute: detection of a single positive bird triggers the mandatory extermination ("depopulation") of the entire flock, with the federal government reimbursing producers through statutory indemnity funds. When European mink farms experienced H5N1 outbreaks in Spain (2022) and Finland (2023), agricultural ministries intervened rapidly, ordering the preemptive culling of hundreds of thousands of animals to eliminate the viral reservoir. In Utah, however, the response was marked by regulatory gaps and jurisdictional confusion: No Federal Authority: The USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) informed Utah state veterinarian Amanda Price that the agency maintains no regulatory framework, dedicated compensation program, or approved vaccines for farmed mink. The USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) informed Utah state veterinarian Amanda Price that the agency maintains no regulatory framework, dedicated compensation program, or approved vaccines for farmed mink. No Formal Quarantine: The Utah Department of Agriculture and Food (UDAF) declined to issue a formal administrative quarantine order. Officials opted instead for an unmonitored "verbal hold," barring the producer from moving animals, manure, or carcasses off-site, while conceding in internal memos they had "no idea what the criteria would be to release" a formal quarantine. Officials opted instead for an unmonitored "verbal hold," barring the producer from moving animals, manure, or carcasses off-site, while conceding in internal memos they had "no idea what the criteria would be to release" a formal quarantine. Physical Absence: State records confirm that Dr. Price never physically inspected the Payson facility during the two-month outbreak, relying entirely on telephone updates with the owner and satellite views from Google Maps. State records confirm that Dr. Price never physically inspected the Payson facility during the two-month outbreak, relying entirely on telephone updates with the owner and satellite views from Google Maps. Industry Influence: Records show agricultural liaisons warned that ordering a cull would bankrupt the producer and destroy decades of selective genetic breeding lines. "The fact that the first instinct wasn't just to depopulate and figure stuff out later is very concerning to me," said Tom Peacock, an avian influenza virologist at the Pirbright Institute. "Every other country that has had H5N1 in fur farms, depopulation has happened pretty quickly." Secrecy and Worker Surveillance Failures State agencies also took active measures to restrict public awareness of the outbreak. Communications between UDAF and the Utah Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) noted that the situation was placed under a "closer hold" than dairy or poultry cases to protect the producer's privacy and avoid alerting animal rights organizations. Even more troubling to public health epidemiologists is the lack of clinical oversight for farmworkers: The Monitoring Ban: Under a 2025 inter-agency operating agreement between Utah's agriculture and health departments, public health officials are prohibited from conducting active symptom monitoring of farm personnel unless human-to-human transmission is already established. Under a 2025 inter-agency operating agreement between Utah's agriculture and health departments, public health officials are prohibited from conducting active symptom monitoring of farm personnel unless human-to-human transmission is already established. Unexamined Symptoms : Agricultural workers on fur operations face high exposure from bites, scratches, and aerosolized spray while handling aggressive animals. During an on-site visit by investigative reporters, an employee at the facility was observed with visible conjunctivitis (eye redness)—a clinical symptom present in more than 90 percent of documented human H5N1 infections. : Agricultural workers on fur operations face high exposure from bites, scratches, and aerosolized spray while handling aggressive animals. During an on-site visit by investigative reporters, an employee at the facility was observed with visible conjunctivitis (eye redness)—a clinical symptom present in more than 90 percent of documented human H5N1 infections. No Diagnostic Testing: The farm owner attributed the irritation to environmental dust, and county health authorities declined to administer diagnostic PCR testing, stating that testing was unnecessary unless the worker developed secondary respiratory symptoms like fever or cough. Federal CDC guidance recommends that all individuals exposed to H5N1-infected mammals undergo active daily health monitoring for ten days following their last contact, with prompt testing for any ocular or respiratory abnormalities. A Shifting Political and Legislative Landscape The Utah outbreak has revived long-standing debates regarding the biosecurity vulnerabilities of the commercial fur trade. During the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, SARS-CoV-2 ripped through nine Utah mink farms, killing nearly 10,000 animals and documenting confirmed transmission between captive mink, feral wildlife, and agricultural workers. In response to the current outbreak, animal protection organizations and public health coalitions are lobbying Congress to pass the Mink VIRUS Act (sponsored by Rep. Adriano Espaillat, D-N.Y.), which would establish a voluntary one-year federal buyout program to permanently phase out domestic mink farming. Conversely, provisions under consideration within the pending federal Farm Bill seek to repeal historic bans on subsidizing the fur sector, opening federal trade promotion funding to domestic pelt producers

supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology H5N1 Avian Influenza Emerges as a Global Threat to Already Declining Vulture Populations by October 28, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 4 mins read 0 H5N1 Avian Influenza Emerges as a Global Threat to Already Declining Vulture Populations Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Vultures, one of the most threatened groups of birds in the world, now face a new and dangerous adversary: the highly pathogenic avian influenza virus H5N1. At least 16 of the 23 vulture species currently recognized are of conservation concern, largely as a result of poisoning and other threats stemming from human activity. Against this already precarious backdrop, the H5N1 virus, which has caused a panzootic, the animal equivalent of a pandemic, is spreading widely in regions that are critical for vultures, and researchers warn that it could push some populations toward collapse. A new letter published in the journal Conservation Biology sets out the scale of the problem and proposes concrete courses of action for conservationists and wildlife managers. The letter was led by Jon Morant, a researcher at the Department of Zoology and Animal Cell Biology of the EHU-University of the Basque Country, working together with several researchers at the Mediterranean Institute for Advanced Studies (IMEDEA) in Mallorca and the Institute for Research in Biodiversity and Environment (INIBIOMA) in Argentina. In addition to Morant, the signatories include Andrea Santangeli of IMEDEA, and Pablo Plaza and Sergio A. Lambertucci of INIBIOMA. Morant, who is also a lecturer and researcher at the Álava Campus of the EHU, is currently undertaking a research stay at the UCD School of Biology and Environmental Science in Dublin as part of a Basque Government postdoctoral programme. The stated aim of the letter is to alert the research community and those responsible for conservation so that they can establish coordinated actions against this emerging threat. The documented impacts of the current H5N1 panzootic on vultures are already severe. Thousands of American black vultures (Coragyps atratus) and Turkey vultures (Cathartes aura) have died in the United States and South America. The virus has also had a significant impact on the Bearded vulture (Gypaetus barbatus) in Europe, and on the California condor (Gymnogyps californianus) and the Andean condor (Vultur gryphus) in the Americas. The situation is particularly alarming for the California condor, a species that is critically endangered: its wild population fell by 6 percent in just six weeks as a result of the outbreak. The ecology of vultures makes them unusually vulnerable to this particular virus. In general, vultures are social animals that gather together at feeding stations, places where the risk of contagion is high because many individuals congregate in close proximity. As scavengers, vultures are resistant to many bacteria and pathogens, an adaptation that allows them to thrive on carrion that would be dangerous to other animals. However, Morant explains, this natural resilience is not enough to protect them from the H5N1 virus, which has a high fatality rate in both domestic and wild animals. Avian influenza is not exclusively a disease of birds. For vultures, the epidemiological logic is stark: the greater the number of infected carcasses in the environment, the greater the risk of contagion for the birds that feed on them. Because these carcasses can themselves become sources of infection, a paradox arises at the population level. As more vultures die, the capacity of the scavenger community to eliminate carrion is reduced, pathogens spread more widely through the environment, and the risk of contagion increases further. This feedback loop means that mortality can, in principle, accelerate rather than stabilize itself, a dynamic that is especially worrying for species already in decline. The threat carries consequences beyond the birds themselves. Vultures provide what Morant describes as one of the most important ecosystem services for human wellbeing: they feed on decomposing animal carcasses that harbour pathogens. It has been proven that scavengers help prevent or reduce the spread of pathogens, in other words, they prevent disease-causing microorganisms from continuing to spread through the environment. A decline in vulture populations therefore removes a natural barrier against the circulation of infectious agents, with potential implications for both wildlife health and human health. This functional role is a central reason why the authors argue that the threat of H5N1 to vultures deserves urgent and coordinated attention from the research and conservation communities. In response, the signatories of the letter call on conservationists and managers to adopt a holistic and multi-dimensional approach to reducing the threat posed to vultures by the H5N1 virus, and they set out five specific courses of action. The first is monitoring: the researchers consider it urgent to monitor vulture populations closely. The second proposed course of action is the implementation of vaccination campaigns when populations are at serious risk and where logistical conditions permit. Morant points to the United States as an example: in the case of the California condor, the research community has implemented a vaccination campaign in response to the high risk of the species becoming extinct. The third course of action concerns the feeding stations used for scavenger birds. Because these sites concentrate large numbers of vultures around supplied carcasses, the authors stress that it is important that the birds are fed with non-contaminated carcasses, so that supplementary feeding does not itself become a route of viral transmission. The fourth course of action is aimed at researchers themselves. The fifth recommendation is to develop and promote action plans adapted to each context. The countries where vultures live have different socio-economic situations and highly diverse governance models, and the authors argue that effective responses must therefore be tailored to local realities rather than imposed as a single uniform template. The signatories are openly concerned about the problem, and they hope that, while the letter remains open, researchers and conservation managers will begin to take action. Morant proposes using the letter as a guide, and concludes that to tackle this dangerous epidemiological situation it is urgent to develop coordinated cross-border plans and to integrate these actions into shared governance structures. The article, titled “Emerging threat of avian influenza to the world’s vultures,” was published in Conservation Biology on 19 August 2026. For a group of birds in which at least 16 of 23 species are already of conservation concern, the arrival of a highly contagious, high-fatality virus that exploits the very scavenging behaviour that makes vultures ecologically valuable represents a threat that the authors argue can only be met through rapid, coordinated and internationally concerted action. Subject of Research: The threat of H5N1 avian influenza to global vulture populations and proposed conservation responses Article Title: Avian influenza threatens vulture populations worldwide Article References: Avian influenza threatens vulture populations worldwide. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Scientists Map Two New Linear Epitopes on H9N2 Bird Flu Hemagglutinin by October 29, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Scientists Map Two New Linear Epitopes on H9N2 Bird Flu Hemagglutinin Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Researchers have identified and precisely mapped two previously uncharacterized linear B-cell epitopes on the hemagglutinin protein of H9N2 avian influenza virus, offering new molecular targets for subtype-specific diagnostic assays. The study, published as an open-access Original Article in the journal Animal Diseases on 22 July 2026, describes the generation of two monoclonal antibodies against the viral HA protein, the fine mapping of the short continuous peptide segments they recognize, and a detailed analysis of the residues and structural contexts that govern antibody binding. Although neither antibody showed neutralizing activity, the authors argue that the epitopes themselves are valuable precisely because they are conserved, surface-exposed, and largely specific to the H9N2 subtype. H9N2 is a low-pathogenicity avian influenza virus that was first isolated from turkeys in Wisconsin, USA, in 1966. Since then it has become endemic in poultry across Asia, the Middle East, Africa, and parts of Europe, and in China it emerged in the 1990s and now ranks among the most prevalent subtypes in chickens and other domestic birds. While infections are typically associated with mild respiratory signs, the virus causes substantial economic losses by reducing egg production, impairing immune function, and increasing susceptibility to secondary bacterial and viral infections. H9N2 also infects a range of avian hosts and occasionally spills over into mammals, including pigs, dogs, and humans, underscoring its zoonotic potential. In addition, the virus frequently donates internal gene segments to other avian influenza subtypes such as H5N1, H7N9, and H10N8, facilitating the emergence of novel reassortant strains with pandemic potential. The hemagglutinin protein sits at the center of both immunity and diagnostics for influenza A viruses. HA functions as a homotrimer on the viral surface, with each monomer consisting of two disulfide-linked subunits: HA1, the globular head that binds sialic acid receptors, and HA2, the stem that mediates membrane fusion. Because HA is strongly immunogenic, it is the principal target of neutralizing antibodies and the backbone of most vaccine and diagnostic antigen design. However, frequent antigenic drift, particularly within the HA1 domain, can alter antibody recognition and erode both vaccine efficacy and the reliability of diagnostic tests. Linear epitopes, which consist of continuous amino acid sequences that remain recognizable even under denaturing conditions, are considered especially useful building blocks for peptide-based diagnostic assays. In the new work, the team, led by Dong Chen and Hongyun Wei with corresponding author Rui Luo, expressed the extracellular domain of HA from the H9N2 strain A/chicken/Hubei/222/2022 as a recombinant fusion protein carrying a human IgG Fc tag. The HA-hFc protein was produced in HEK293 cells and purified by protein A affinity chromatography. SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis revealed a single band above the predicted molecular weight of roughly 90 kilodaltons, a shift consistent with glycosylation, and Western blotting with H9N2-specific mouse antiserum and an anti-human IgG reagent confirmed successful expression and purification of the immunogen. Immunization of BALB/c mice with this recombinant protein yielded two hybridoma clones, designated 9C12 and 9F4. Both monoclonal antibodies specifically recognized viral HA in H9N2-infected MDCK cells, as demonstrated by Western blotting and an indirect immunofluorescence assay, and both bound the recombinant antigen in ELISA. Functional testing, however, showed that neither antibody inhibited hemagglutination in a hemagglutination inhibition assay, and neutralization assays returned IC50 values greater than 50 micrograms per milliliter, indicating that no neutralizing activity was detectable in vitro. The antibodies therefore recognize antigenically accessible but non-neutralizing regions of the HA molecule, a profile the authors consider well suited to epitope mapping and diagnostic development rather than therapeutic or vaccine applications. To locate the exact binding sites, the researchers used a panel of N-terminal EGFP-tagged HA truncation constructs expressed in HEK293T cells and screened by Western blot. For 9C12, sequential subdivision narrowed the reactive region from the full HA1 domain, amino acids 19 to 338, down through fragments covering residues 96 to 195, 96 to 145, and 116 to 135, before overlapping short peptides defined the minimal linear epitope as the eight-residue sequence FSSSRSYQ at positions 123 to 130. The same strategy applied to 9F4 traced its binding site through HA1 subfragments of residues 176 to 279, 176 to 225, and 196 to 215, ultimately defining the minimal epitope as the nine-residue sequence NLYTRTDTT at positions 201 to 209. Alanine-scanning mutagenesis then resolved which individual residues within each epitope are essential for antibody recognition. Within the 9C12 epitope, replacing S124, S125, R127, S128, Y129, or Q130 with alanine abolished antibody binding, whereas substitutions at F123 and S126 had no detectable effect. For the 9F4 epitope, the indispensable residues were N201, Y203, T204, T206, and D207, while L202, R205, T208, and T209 could be replaced without disrupting recognition. These single-residue definitions, the authors note, provide a rational molecular basis for assay design, since the critical positions are predominantly hydrophilic or charged, consistent with their role as anchor points stabilizing the antibody-epitope interaction. Structural and bioinformatic analyses placed both epitopes in functional context. Immunological profiling with the PROTEAN module of DNAStar showed that both peptides display strong hydrophilicity, high antigenic indices, and elevated surface probability. A three-dimensional homology model of the HA trimer, generated with SWISS-MODEL and based on the A/chicken/Hubei/222/2022 sequence, confirmed that both epitopes are exposed on the surface of the trimer and solvent accessible. Domain-level mapping revealed that the 9F4 epitope NLYTRTDTT lies within the receptor-binding subdomain, whereas the 9C12 epitope FSSSRSYQ resides in the vestigial esterase subdomain. Notably, even though the 9F4 epitope sits within the receptor-binding region, its recognition by 9F4 was insufficient to confer detectable neutralizing activity. Conservation analysis strengthened the diagnostic case for both motifs. Multiple sequence alignment of HA proteins from 30 representative H9N2 isolates retrieved from the NCBI database showed that the 9C12 epitope is largely conserved, with key residues F123, S124, S125, S128, Y129, and Q130 strongly stable and only minor substitutions observed at S126 and R127. The 9F4 epitope, by contrast, displayed near-complete invariance across all strains analyzed, which the authors describe as exceptional stability within the H9N2 subtype. When the same regions were compared with homologous sequences in other influenza A virus subtypes, including H1 through H13 and H16, both epitopes were poorly conserved in non-H9 viruses, suggesting subtype-associated conservation that could serve as a molecular marker for H9N2-associated detection and surveillance. The authors position these findings against the limitations of current serological tools. Traditional hemagglutination inhibition tests remain widely used but are often limited by cross-reactivity and insufficient resolution when distinguishing closely related subtypes such as H9, H5, and H7. Monoclonal antibodies directed against short, well-defined linear epitopes such as NLYTRTDTT may help improve the specificity of H9N2 serological detection, a capability relevant to field surveillance, vaccine strain selection, outbreak containment, and monitoring of antigenic evolution. The authors emphasize that because both epitopes are nonneutralizing, they are unsuitable for direct use in protective vaccine design, and they caution that future work must validate diagnostic performance across large-scale poultry samples and multiple assay platforms, including peptide-based ELISAs and lateral-flow immunoassays. Within those limits, the study delivers experimentally validated peptide motifs and paired monoclonal antibodies that expand the antigenic map of H9N2 hemagglutinin and provide concrete raw material for subtype-specific diagnostic reagents. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Universal influenza vaccine platforms advance toward broader H5N1 pandemic readiness by October 28, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 7 mins read 0 Universal influenza vaccine platforms advance toward broader H5N1 pandemic readiness Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A newly published review in Discover Immunity examines how universal influenza vaccine platforms could strengthen the world’s defenses against H5N1 avian influenza, a virus the authors describe as a significant threat to global public health. The review, published on 4 October 2026 as an open-access article, brings together current evidence on licensed and experimental H5N1 vaccines, the immunological factors that shape their performance, and the manufacturing and distribution systems that would determine whether an effective response to an outbreak is even possible. Its central argument is that protection against a virus as antigenically variable as H5N1 cannot rest on strain-matched vaccines alone, but requires platforms built around conserved regions of the virus that can generate durable, cross-protective immunity against multiple variants. The review begins by situating H5N1 within the broader landscape of zoonotic threats. H5N1 avian influenza is described as a particularly dangerous strain of influenza A virus because it can infect both birds and humans. First identified in Hong Kong in 1997, the virus has since caused periodic outbreaks in poultry and wild birds across global regions, with occasional human infections that have had fatal consequences. Highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses kill large quantities of poultry and impose significant economic losses on the poultry industry worldwide. In humans, the review notes, H5N1 infection can lead to acute respiratory distress and organ failure, with a fatality rate described as extremely high compared with seasonal influenza strains. Human infections occur mainly through close contact with infected chickens or contaminated environments, and the possibility that mutations could enable sustained human-to-human transmission remains a central concern. The virus’s rapid mutation rate and its potential for human-to-human spread are cited as the reasons it has become a priority for global health surveillance and preparedness. Against this background, the review assesses what current H5N1 vaccine platforms actually deliver. Licensed, prepandemic and stockpiled H5N1 vaccines are inactivated and recombinant hemagglutinin vaccines, developed with or without adjuvants. The immunogenicity literature indicates that adjuvanted preparations consistently induce higher hemagglutination inhibition and neutralizing antibody titers than non-adjuvanted preparations, and reach seroprotective titers, defined as an HAI titer of at least 1:40, with lower antigen doses and fewer injections. Oil-in-water adjuvants such as AS03 and MF59 stimulate B cell responses to antigens and engage T follicular helper cells, increasing the extent and persistence of humoral immune responses. Strain-specific neutralization is strong with inactivated adjuvanted vaccines when the vaccine matches the circulating H5N1 clade, but cross-reactivity against heterologous clades is inconsistent and mostly inferior. Recombinant hemagglutinin vaccines containing conserved stalk epitopes show slight enhancement of cross-clade responses, yet neutralizing titers against divergent H5N1 subclades often fall below presumptive protective thresholds without booster immunizations. A crucial limitation the review emphasizes is the near-total absence of real-world effectiveness data. Because there has been no sustained human-to-human transmission of H5N1, H5N1 vaccines have generated few field effectiveness data, and licensure and stockpiling decisions have instead relied on surrogate endpoints, namely immunogenicity correlates such as HAI and neutralization titers. Pre-licensure clinical experience in high-risk groups such as poultry workers shows acceptable safety and immunogenicity, but conclusive protective effectiveness against natural H5N1 infection has not been determined. The authors conclude that although these vaccines achieve high immunogenicity against homologous strains when boosted with adjuvant, their heterologous breadth is poor, and no real-world effectiveness data currently exist to support vaccine optimization and real-time assessment during an actual outbreak. The review then turns to next-generation candidates designed for safety, immunogenicity and cross-protection. It describes H5N1 as now an established, year-round infection whose host range has expanded to include many mammals. The virus’s pathogenicity is attributed mainly to the acquisition of a polybasic hemagglutinin cleavage site, which facilitates systemic spread, alongside emerging endothelial and neurotropic properties that produce severe disease and high mortality in mammals. H5N1 has been observed to accumulate mutations linked to mammalian adaptation, albeit with limited transmission, notably in the hemagglutinin and polymerase complex. Novel mammalian reservoirs, including dairy cattle in the United States, raise human exposure risk. In response, vaccine development is shifting from older adjuvanted inactivated vaccines toward new platforms, with mRNA and virus-like particle vaccines being developed for rapid rollout and broader immune responses. The review highlights the speed of mRNA production, achievable in weeks from sequence reads, as making it one of the most promising pandemic platforms. Several experimental strategies receive detailed attention. Live attenuated influenza virus vaccines based on NS segment truncation prevent influenza virus infection and have shown promise as vaccine candidates among other platforms, though the authors argue that more attention must turn to LAIV development platforms to produce a truly universal influenza vaccine candidate. H5 antigens expressed by recombinant adenovirus and vesicular stomatitis virus vectors induce robust humoral and cellular immunity in individuals after single vaccinations; non-replicating adenoviral vectors have proven safe, while replicating VSV platforms can activate stronger innate responses. Pre-existing anti-vector immunity is a recognized consideration, which heterologous prime-boost regimens can alleviate. Structure-guided design uses computational algorithms to stabilize hemagglutinin in its pre-fusion conformation or to display conserved epitopes, and computationally optimized broadly reactive antigens, known as COBRAs, extend cross-clade neutralization by concentrating on conserved regions. These antigens can be deployed across delivery systems including mRNA and protein formats. Universal strategies targeting the conserved hemagglutinin stem, the matrix protein 2 ectodomain, or internal proteins such as NP and M1 aim to induce cross-subtype protection, while chimeric hemagglutinin constructs, mosaic nanoparticles and multi-epitope chimeras are designed to address the antigenic diversity of H5 lineages. Despite these efforts, the review notes a persistent lack of broadly reactive antibody induction capable of conferring broad, long-lasting protection. The review also examines what determines whether an H5N1 vaccine works in a given person or population. AS03-adjuvanted H5N1 vaccine generates substantially more potent immune responses than non-adjuvanted vaccine, and one study found the adjuvant may boost responses by switching off the NR4A1 and SDC1 genes, switching on the ID3 gene and decreasing cortisol production, although the mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Two-dose schedules with a three-week interval have induced high neutralizing antibody levels against the vaccine strain, and protection may persist for up to three years after two doses of AS03-adjuvanted H5N1 vaccines, with the prime-boost schedule producing robust anamnestic antibody responses that are cross-protective. However, prior antigenic imprinting, or original antigenic sin, can shape future responses: B cell repertoires focus on conserved epitopes from initial exposure, which may suppress responses to new antigenic variants and limit the breadth of neutralizing responses, potentially reducing seroconversion to drifted antigens. Host genetics also matter, as single-nucleotide polymorphisms in pattern recognition receptors such as TLR7 and TLR8 and in cytokine regulators determine the magnitude of antibody and T cell responses. Immunosenescence reduces both humoral and cellular responses, with most older adults showing reduced HAI titers after vaccination, and comorbidities such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease and immunosuppression further lower responsiveness. On the viral side, antigenic drift in hemagglutinin and neuraminidase can produce circulating strains that no longer match vaccine antigens, reassortment can generate combinations against which pre-existing immunity offers minimal protection, and suboptimal poultry vaccination coverage can select drifted variants in reservoirs, complicating human vaccine strain selection and raising zoonotic spillover risk. Adjuvants emerge as a key lever for improving and shaping immunity. Oil-in-water adjuvants such as AS03 and MF59 enable reduced antigen doses while achieving high seroconversion by improving antigen uptake by antigen-presenting cells and triggering strong innate signaling, a dose-sparing capability the review considers especially valuable when pandemic production capacity is limited. Adjuvants activate diverse B cell clones and drive antibody affinity maturation, which may expand cross-clade neutralization breadth against antigenically drifted H5N1 strains, an important property for prepandemic stockpiles where the future strain cannot be predicted. Newer adjuvant preparations containing toll-like receptor agonists and synthetic immunomodulators are engineered to favor balanced Th1 and Th2 responses. In older adults and immunocompromised individuals, who commonly respond poorly to unadjuvanted vaccines, higher doses of adjuvants that strongly activate innate immunity, such as TLR4 agonists and saponin formulations, can partially address these limitations by enhancing dendritic cell activation and cytokine milieus. The review cautions that reactogenicity, including local pain and temporary systemic responses, must be assessed, and that while AS03 and MF59 have shown generally acceptable safety in controlled studies, continued surveillance across different populations is crucial. On evaluation methods, the review describes a tiered pathway. Preclinical tests in mice, ferrets and non-human primates establish safety, immunogenicity and protective effect, with ferrets considered the best influenza model because their respiratory anatomy and disease progression resemble those of humans. Hemagglutination inhibition titers remain a key correlate of protection, neutralization tests measure the strength of serum antibodies against viral entry, and cellular immunity assays such as ELISpot and intracellular cytokine staining quantify T cell responses associated with viral clearance and cross-clade coverage. Robust correlates accelerate development by reducing reliance on large efficacy trials that are ethically or logistically infeasible in prepandemic phases. Phase III randomized controlled trials in target populations typically use laboratory-confirmed influenza illness as the endpoint, and after approval, observational studies including cohort, case-control and test-negative designs assess real-world performance against circulating strains. Recent work illustrates the pipeline: an mRNA vaccine expressing the hemagglutinin of the first bovine-to-human strain, A/Texas/37/2024, stimulated strong, long-lasting humoral responses and a balanced Th1/Th2 profile in murine studies, providing 100 percent protection against lethal homologous challenge, and produced cross-clade binding antibody responses with a favorable safety profile in rats. Separately, an H5N1 vaccine cultured in serum-free MDCK cell suspension protected mice in challenge tests, with antibodies persisting up to eight months after the first dose in rats and elevated IP-10 levels indicating enhanced innate immunity. The review closes by linking vaccine science to delivery and equity. Intradermal delivery targets the immune cells of the skin and can achieve strong responses with lower antigen doses, extending scarce vaccine supplies, though it requires specialized equipment and trained personnel. Microneedle patches offer needle-free, self-administered vaccination with thermostability that removes cold-chain constraints, although mass production and regulatory licensing remain hurdles. Mucosal intranasal vaccines induce both systemic and mucosal immunity at the respiratory entry point but face stability and formulation issues. Heterologous prime-boost regimens, such as intramuscular priming followed by mucosal boosting, may make immunity more durable and broader against variants. The authors argue that equitable global distribution frameworks such as COVAX must ensure vaccines reach low- and middle-income countries based on need, with high-risk groups prioritized. Combined, they conclude, universal vaccines targeting conserved regions, durable cross-protection, agile manufacturing and fair distribution form the strategy they identify as most capable of reducing the threat of an H5N1 pandemic and improving global preparedness. Subject of Research: Universal influenza vaccine platforms for H5N1 pandemic preparedness Article Title: Recent advances in universal influenza vaccine platforms: paving the way for universal H5N1 vaccines and pandemic readiness Article References: Ali, S., Bibi, H., Ullah, H., Mehmood, M. S., Kamal, M. A., & Nazari, M. J. (2026). Recent advances in universal influenza vaccine platforms: paving the way for universal H5N1 vaccines and pandemic readiness. supplementary_news.content: Toggle navigation AGDAILY – Your Source for Agriculture News, Trends, & Videos Results Quick Links FFA News & Features Ag Insider Diversity in Agriculture Mental Wellness in Ag Farm Babe Columns Signup Resources Beginning Farmers Grants & Loans FFA College Guide Diversity in Ag Sections News Lifestyle Weather Crops Livestock Technology Diversity in Ag Featured News Insights Columnists Agri-Pulse News FFA Signup Work With Us These rural place names are downright hellish By Sarah Alexander Melotte, The Daily Yonder Read More Read Halloween candy prices soar, but sugar farmers aren’t seeing gains Read Rollins pressures remaining states to join diesel relief effort Read Screwworm reaches Arizona as cases spread across Southwest Agriculture news Oct 29, 2026 Crops ● Lifestyle Read AGDAILY Reporters Halloween candy prices soar, but sugar farmers aren’t seeing gains Halloween candy prices have climbed dramatically over the past several decades, but the American Sugar Alliance says the farmers producing one of candy’s key ingredients aren’t seeing the same increases. According to the organization’s annual grocery store price survey, consumers are paying 397 percent more for a standard chocolate bar than they were a generation ago. Meanwhile, the alliance says the cost of the sugar used in that same chocolate bar has remained relatively unchanged. The comparison comes as Americans prepare for another expensive Halloween. The National Retail Federation projects that 96 percent of Halloween shoppers will purchase candy this year, with spending expected to reach $4.1 billion. Despite higher prices at grocery store checkouts, the American Sugar Alliance says the sugar in a typical chocolate bar still accounts for just a few cents of its retail price. The organization, which represents U.S. sugarbeet and sugarcane growers, processors, and refiners, argues that rising candy prices have not translated into comparable gains for domestic sugar producers. The alliance’s figures also raise questions about what’s driving higher retail candy prices. Sugar is only one component of candy production costs, alongside cocoa, dairy ingredients, labor, packaging, transportation, and manufacturing. Higher retail prices do not necessarily mean larger profits for candy manufacturers, either. While the alliance’s survey illustrates the growing gap between candy prices and sugar costs, it does not establish how much of the increase can be attributed to individual ingredients or other expenses. Image courtesy of the American Sugar Alliance U.S. sugar producers face mounting pressure Beyond Halloween candy prices, the American Sugar Alliance is drawing attention to challenges facing domestic sugarbeet and sugarcane operations. The organization argues that subsidized foreign sugar entering the U.S. market is displacing domestic production and putting downward pressure on prices received by American producers. “If subsidized foreign sugar is permitted to continue to flood the market, displacing U.S. production and depressing prices, it will be a nightmare for all Americans as we face the loss of more American sugarbeet and sugarcane farms and factories,” the alliance said. The group pointed to the disappearance of sugar production in several states as evidence of the industry’s struggles. Hawaii ended commercial sugarcane production in 2016, followed by Texas in 2024. California’s sugarbeet production ended in 2025, according to the alliance. Those closures highlight the challenges of maintaining domestic sugar production amid changing market conditions, production expenses, and international competition. Image courtesy of the American Sugar Alliance However, the alliance’s criticism of foreign sugar comes from an organization that advocates for policies supporting domestic producers. The U.S. sugar industry also operates under a federal support program that includes import restrictions, marketing allotments, and price-support loans. Those policies are intended to support domestic production, although critics argue they can keep U.S. sugar prices above world market levels. The alliance maintains that protecting American sugar production is important for preserving agricultural jobs, processing infrastructure, and domestic food supply chains. “The farm families who grow sugarbeets and sugarcane are a critical part of the American food supply,” the organization said. For consumers filling Halloween candy bowls, the price of sweets continues to rise. For sugar farmers, the alliance argues, the more pressing concern is whether domestic production can remain economically viable. Share Oct 29, 2026 Poultry Read AGDAILY Reporters AI could change how poultry producers feed their flocks Artificial intelligence is finding its way into another corner of agriculture, and researchers say poultry nutrition could be among the next areas to benefit. By combining real-time monitoring, large datasets, and machine learning, scientists believe producers could better match feed formulations to the changing nutritional needs of their birds, potentially reducing feed costs, waste, and environmental impacts. A new research review from Jilin University, China Agricultural University, and the Jilin Academy of Agricultural Sciences examines how artificial intelligence and emerging biotechnology could improve precision feeding in commercial poultry production. The study, titled Integration of Big Data and AI Empowered Precision Poultry Nutrition: A Review, explores how technologies already gaining traction in livestock production could be used together to make poultry feeding more responsive to individual flocks and changing production conditions. Feed represents one of the largest operating expenses in poultry production, making even modest improvements in feed efficiency potentially valuable for commercial operations. Traditional poultry nutrition programs rely heavily on established nutrient requirements, feed ingredient analyses, and mathematical models to formulate diets. Although these methods have supported decades of productivity improvements, they cannot always account for differences in bird physiology, environmental conditions, or changing nutritional requirements throughout the production cycle. Researchers argue that artificial intelligence could help address those limitations by analyzing far more variables than conventional models can efficiently process. Machine learning algorithms can evaluate relationships among feed ingredients, nutrient availability, bird performance, and environmental conditions to improve predictions of dietary energy values and nutritional requirements. The researchers found that these approaches offer advantages over traditional linear regression models, particularly when dealing with complex biological relationships and changing production environments. Rather than relying exclusively on predetermined feeding recommendations, producers could eventually use continuously updated information to adjust diets as flock conditions change. Sensors and cameras could help guide feeding decisions A major component of the proposed approach involves connecting artificial intelligence with technologies capable of collecting information directly from poultry houses. Sensors, computer vision systems, and internet-connected monitoring equipment can provide information about environmental conditions, bird behavior, and production performance. When combined with machine learning, these datasets could help identify changes in nutritional needs or performance before they become obvious through conventional monitoring. For example, information about feed consumption, growth patterns, and house conditions could be analyzed together to identify opportunities for dietary adjustments. The researchers also examined the potential of combining artificial intelligence with omics technologies, which study biological systems such as genes, proteins, and metabolites. These tools could provide a more detailed understanding of how poultry metabolize nutrients and why birds respond differently to particular feed formulations. The review also considers biotechnology-derived proteins as potential components of future poultry feeding systems. Together, these technologies could support diets designed around more detailed biological information rather than relying solely on broader flock-level nutritional estimates. Potential savings come with practical questions Researchers suggest that more precise feeding could reduce unnecessary nutrient supplementation, improve feed conversion, and lower production costs. Better matching dietary protein and energy levels to actual requirements could also reduce nutrient waste and nitrogen excretion, while potentially lowering the environmental footprint associated with feed production. However, the research is a review of existing technologies and scientific findings, rather than a commercial feeding trial demonstrating a specific reduction in costs or emissions. That distinction matters for poultry producers evaluating whether these technologies are worth adopting. Although machine learning models may outperform conventional approaches in predicting certain nutritional variables, improved predictions do not automatically translate into better financial returns under commercial production conditions. Implementing these systems could require investments in sensors, monitoring equipment, software, data management, and technical expertise. Producers would also need reliable information about feed ingredients and bird performance for the models to generate useful recommendations. Questions remain about how well algorithms developed using particular breeds, diets, or production environments would perform across different commercial operations. Data quality presents another challenge. Incomplete or inaccurate measurements could undermine the recommendations generated by even sophisticated artificial intelligence systems. And while the researchers identify potential environmental benefits, the extent of those improvements would depend on how effectively the technologies are implemented and whether producers can achieve measurable changes in feed efficiency and nutrient losses. What it could mean for poultry production Precision nutrition is not a new concept in animal agriculture. Poultry nutritionists already use detailed ingredient analyses, nutritional models, and production data to develop feeding programs. What artificial intelligence could change is the speed and complexity of those decisions. Instead of making adjustments primarily at predetermined production stages, future systems could potentially recommend changes based on continuously collected flock information. For large commercial operations, where small differences in feed efficiency can translate into substantial expenses across millions of birds, the potential economic implications are significant. Still, the technology’s value will ultimately depend on whether it can deliver consistent, measurable improvements that justify the cost of adoption. The researchers conclude that integrating artificial intelligence, big data, and biotechnology could provide a foundation for more efficient and environmentally sustainable poultry production. For producers, the next step will be determining how much of that promise holds up in commercial poultry houses, where profitability, animal welfare, and practical management requirements must all be considered. Share Oct 29, 2026 Crops Read AGDAILY Rollins pressures remaining states to join diesel relief effort U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins on Thursday commended the 31 states acting in concert with the Trump administration’s emergency dyed diesel relief effort and called on the remaining governors to follow suit before the end of harvest. The relief traces to Executive Order 14435, Emergency Tax Relief on Diesel Fuel, which President Donald Trump signed on October 5. The order directs the U.S. Department of the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service to grant temporary federal penalty relief for on-highway use of off-road dyed diesel and to suspend enforcement of the applicable federal excise taxes. The federal diesel excise tax runs 24.4 cents per gallon, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture projects the wider effort could produce in excess of $640 million in combined federal and state savings spanning an estimated 224.6 million acres of harvested cropland. “I want to personally thank President Trump and Vice President Vance for their leadership in advancing this important relief for American agriculture. I also want to commend the governors who have taken action to provide relief to our hardworking farmers, ranchers, and transportation operators during this critical harvest season,” Rollins said. “For the remaining states, I respectfully encourage their governors to join us in taking corresponding action on dyed diesel alongside the Trump Administration.” A combine makes a pass in Colfax, North Dakota. (Image by tony Franzwa, Shutterstock) IRS guidance spells out enforcement suspension Acting on the president’s directive, the IRS published guidance (IR-2026-122) on October 14, 2026, that suspends collection and enforcement of the federal dyed diesel excise tax while the relief window remains open and waives the on-road use penalty. A second round of guidance (IR-2026-125), released October 21, 2026, eased federal reporting and recordkeeping obligations on covered dyed diesel transactions for the same window. As of now, 31 states have put in place or announced dyed-diesel measures, among them suspending certain penalties, adjusting enforcement practices, or taking other action meant to ease burdens on agricultural producers and transportation operators. The USDA said it will keep working alongside state leaders to support implementation. Farmers, ranchers, fuel distributors, and state officials with questions on eligibility or implementation can contact the USDA at DyedDiesel@usda.gov or consult the IRS’s Dyed Diesel Frequently Asked Questions. This article was prepared with the assistance of automated tools and human research and verified by our editorial team. The dog was receiving veterinary treatment. “We have been preparing for this possibility for a long while and are acting swiftly,” Arizona State Veterinarian Dr. Ryan Wolker said. “Because of the extensive outreach, coordination and surveillance already in place, Arizona producers, veterinarians and pet owners know what to look for and how to report suspected cases. That preparation is allowing us to move quickly to protect animal health in the state.” The detection comes as federal and state officials contend with an increasing number of infestations across the Southwest, including recent cases involving cattle, sheep, pets and wildlife. Check animals daily for: ✔️ Draining or enlarging wounds ✔️ Maggots or egg masses ✔️ Signs of discomfort ✔️ Lesions around the ears, nose, genital area, or umbilicus If you suspect NWS, contact your veterinarian, state animal health official, or USDA immediately. Thursday, October 29, 2026 Preprint: Why Americans Choose Raw Milk: Evidence from a National Quantitative Survey #19,391 With reports of H5N1 infected dairy herds increasing again (see Washington State: H5N1 Detections in Cattle Triple (n=27) - 2nd County (Benton) Affected), we are seeing an uptick in warnings from health departments about the dangers of consuming raw milk. The King County, WA Dept. of Public Health unambiguously warns: Raw (unpasteurized) milk and raw milk products Consuming raw milk and raw milk products can pose health risks. Raw milk and A(H5N1) virus The CDC recommends against consuming raw milk contaminated with live A(H5N1) virus as a way to develop antibodies against A(H5N1) virus to protect against future disease. Consuming raw milk could make you sick. Why is raw milk unsafe? Raw milk is milk from animals, typically cows and goats, which has not been pasteurized. Pasteurization is a process of heating raw milk to kill germs from the animal that are present in the raw milk. Some people believe that raw milk is more nutritious than pasteurized milk; however, the major nutrients in milk are not affected by pasteurization. Raw milk and raw milk products, such as cream, cheese and yogurt can be contaminated with harmful bacteria and cause serious infections. People with weakened immune systems, young children, the elderly, and pregnant women are at increased risk for severe infections from raw milk and milk products. It is especially important that young children, elderly persons, and persons with weakened immune systems consume only pasteurized milk and milk products. Read the label! In Washington state, it is legal to sell raw milk but raw milk products must be clearly labeled. In the fall of 2024, we saw similar warnings after a number of household pets were infected with H5N1, some presumably from exposure to raw milk and/or raw pet food (see LA County Issues Another Raw Milk Warning). Despite ample evidence of its dangers, most states allow its sale from farms or co-ops, and some states - like Washington - allow it to be sold in grocery stores alongside pasteurized milk. State Laws on sale of raw milk - Credit CDC A 2022 study published in the Journal of Food Protection found that: Results show that 4.4% of U.S. adults reported consuming raw milk at least once in the past year, with 1.6% reporting frequent consumption of raw milk (once per month or more often) and 1.0% reporting consumption once per week or more often. Today we have a new preprint - published Oct 28th - which suggests Americans' consumption of raw milk may be even higher than previously reported. It is based on a survey of 1,075 eligible US adults through an online panel in February of 2025, and it reports roughly 15% of US adults consumed raw milk in the preceding six months. While it is possible that pro-raw-milk enthusiasts were more likely to respond to this survey, recruitment was done through Qualtrics Research Services - using demographic quotas - not an openly advertised public poll. I've posted the abstract below, but those wishing a deeper dive will want to follow the link to read the preprint in its entirety. Why Americans Choose Raw Milk: Evidence from a National Quantitative Survey Sophia Ruser, Cristina Rojo, Katherine J Koebel, Calvin Slaughter, Ece Bulut, Renata Ivanek doi: https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.10.26.26366487 This article is a preprint and has not been certified by peer review Preview PDF Abstract Raw milk consumption is a controllable source of foodborne pathogen exposure in the United States (US), yet existing national estimates of raw milk consumption behaviors are outdated and do not capture emerging factors such as consumers' trusted information sources, sociopolitical influences, and at-home risk mitigation behaviors. We conducted a nationally representative cross-sectional survey of n=1078 US adults to estimate the prevalence of raw milk consumption and at-home thermal treatment practices and identify predictors of these behaviors. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to evaluate predictors of raw milk consumption and thermal treatment behavior using adjusted odds ratios (aORs). Among 1,075 eligible respondents, 15% consumed raw milk in the last six months, including 5% exclusively and 10% in addition to pasteurized milk. In multivariable analysis, raw milk consumption was independently associated with younger age, cohabitation with high-risk individuals for foodborne infections (including children less than or equal to five years of age, and elderly, pregnant or immunocompromised individuals) who had consumed raw milk, and perceptions of raw milk taste and safety. Adults aged greater than or equal to 55 years had lower odds of consumption than those aged 18-24 years (aOR, 0.05; 95% CI, 0.02-0.15), while those living with a high-risk household member who consumed raw milk had higher odds of consumption (aOR, 4.39; 95% CI, 2.69-7.22). Perceiving raw milk to have higher risk of causing illness was associated with lower odds of raw milk consumption (aOR: 0.32, 95% CI: 0.17-0.62) compared to believing the risk to be equal across milk types, and thermal treatment was reported by 38% of exclusive raw milk consumers (n=58) and 47% of consumers of both milk types (n=106). Raw milk consumption in the US appears to be substantially more common than previously reported and shaped by factors such as taste, safety, and household raw milk consumption among high-risk individuals for foodborne infections. The proportion of raw milk consumers already practicing at-home thermal treatment suggests a potential opportunity for risk mitigation. While all of this is self-reported and unverified information, it appears that among the respondents to this poll that high-risk groups (young children, elderly persons, and persons with weakened immune systems) are often cited as household consumers of raw milk. 10.0% reported a child aged five or younger who had consumed it. 9.1% reported an adult aged 65 or older. 3.2% reported an immunocompromised person. 2.1% reported a pregnant person. One potential bright spot, however, is the reported practice of heating or steaming raw milk (44% reported doing so > 50% of the time). Whether their heating temperatures and times were sufficient to kill pathogens is unknown. Since we've seen multiple instances where H5N1 contaminated raw milk has reached store shelves (see California: CDFA Announces Another Recall of H5 Contaminated Raw Milk), the risks - while low - are genuine. But whether any of this will dissuade those currently inclined to consume raw milk - after decades of near universal public health advice to the contrary - remains to be seen. Wednesday, October 28, 2026 WHO: Fatal H1N1v Infection In Brazil #19,390 Overnight the World Health Organization published its latest Influenza at the human-animal interface summary and assessment, 7 October 2026, which describes one previously reported H5N1 case from Cambodia, 4 recent H9N2 cases reported from Mainland China, and one fatal H1N1v case from Brazil. The H1N1v case is unusual in that the adult female patient - who had (unspecified) pre-existing chronic conditions - died after a month-long hospitalization. Of note: Her husband and three adult children also reported flu-like symptoms - were treated for a `viral infection' - but were never tested. According to the timeline provided by this report, the hospitalized case was only identified as having a novel flu (H1N1v) a week after her death. As a result, epidemiological investigation wasn't begun until September 5th, roughly 7 weeks after she (and her family) first fell ill. First, the WHO report, after which I'll return with more. Swine influenza viruses in humans Influenza A(H1N1)v, Brazil On 30 September 2026, Brazil notified PAHO/WHO of a laboratory-confirmed human infection with an influenza A(H1N1)v virus in an adult woman, with pre-existing chronic conditions, residing in the state of Santa Catarina. She developed symptoms of influenza-like illness on 16 July 2026 and sought medical attention on 20 July. Her husband and three adult children, who live in the same household,also experienced symptoms of an influenza-like illness; at that time, all were diagnosed, based solely on clinical examination, with a viral infection and received treatment. The woman, however, did not recover. On 27 July, the patient was hospitalized due to worsening respiratory symptoms. She received treatment, including the antiviral oseltamivir, and required intensive care, including ventilatory support. Despite intensive care, the patient passed away on 28 August. A nasopharyngeal sample, collected on 29 July, tested positive for influenza A on 30 July and was subsequently subtyped as influenza A(H1N1) on 31 July. The sample was sent to the reference laboratory for respiratory viruses at the Oswaldo Cruz Institute (IOC/Fiocruz) in Rio de Janeiro for further characterization. On 4 September, genomic analysis identified an influenza A(H1N1)v virus. According to information gathered during an epidemiological investigation conducted by municipal and state teams between 5 and 9 September, the patient had no history of travel or direct contact with swine. However, a possible indirect exposure to swine was identified through a neighbour who raises these animals for personal consumption. Since 2015, twelve cases of human infection with swine-origin virus variants, including this one, have been detected within Brazil’s respiratory virus surveillance workflow. This chronology illustrates just how difficult it can be to detect a novel virus, even when the patient is hospitalized with severe influenza. A few recent examples include: In November of 2025, Washington State reported the first known human infection with avian H5N5; a diagnosis that was delayed - according to an MMWR report - by `early and repeated negative influenza test results from upper respiratory swab specimens'. In 2024, a Missouri patient was hospitalized with influenza A, and released, before being notified they had H5N1 (see Missouri DHSS: Human H5 bird flu case confirmed in Missouri). Also in 2024, Australia treated a child with recent travel from India for severe flu, which resulted in respiratory failure. The child fell ill (in India) in late February, was hospitalized in Melbourne in early March, and was released after > 2 weeks. While respiratory samples were taken in early March, they weren't identified as H5N1 positive until mid-May. Complicating matters, most people experiencing mild or moderate flu symptoms are unlikely to seek medical care, and even when they do, they are often treated for a `viral illness' and never tested. We've seen past studies (see here, here, and here) suggesting that as few as 1 in 100 cases are identified in the community. In early 2025, the CDC issued a HAN: Accelerated Subtyping of Influenza A in Hospitalized Patients, requesting that all hospitalized patients with suspected influenza be subtyped within 24 hours. More recently, we saw Washington State: Updated guidance for novel influenza screening and influenza subtyping, which emphasized the importance of identifying those with acute respiratory illness (ARI) and specific epidemiologic risk factors. The reality is, it takes a certain degree of luck to detect sporadic novel flu infections in the community. While better screening methods could improve detection rates, many mild and moderate infections will still likely fly beneath our radar. A reminder than anything we say about the current threat from H5N1, swine flu variants, MERS-CoV, or any other pandemic threat must carry an implied asterisk. A disclaimer that says, ` * based on available, and likely incomplete, information. . . '. Tuesday, October 27, 2026 Washington State: H5N1 Detections in Cattle Triple (n=27) - 2nd County (Benton) Affected #18,389 While it hasn't shown up yet on the USDA's H5N1 in Livestock dashboard, the number of dairy herds in Washington State infected with HPAI has jumped from 9 late last week, to 27, with a second county (Benton) now reporting an infected herd. Less than 3 weeks ago (Oct 8th) the USDA/APHIS announced the first detection of H5N1 in dairy cattle in Washington State, which was followed a week later by the first (reportedly mild) human H5N1 infection reported in the U.S. in 2026 (see Washington State Confirms Human Avian Flu Infection). Other than the (above) update to the Washington State Dept. Agriculture dashboard, I have found no other public announcement of this jump in detections. Yesterday, the WSDA did publish a statement on the detection of H5N1 in a second county, which also states: Media note: WSDA will issue a news release for each new county with confirmed HPAI in cattle. Subsequent detections in previously announced counties will be posted online. Excerpts from yesterday's announcement follow: WSDA confirms HPAI in dairy herd in Benton County OLYMPIA – Oct. 26, 2026 – Washington State Department of Agriculture (WSDA) has confirmed a detection of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 in a Benton County dairy herd. The virus was detected by the Washington Animal Disease Diagnostic Laboratory (WADDL) through routine surveillance, and the finding was confirmed by the USDA National Veterinary Services Laboratories (NVSL). The dairy herd is under quarantine and has employed strict biosecurity measures. Veterinarians are working to treat sick cows. Pasteurized milk products remain safe for consumers, and milk supply shortages are not expected. WSDA urges dairy farmers statewide to report any clinical signs of illness to their veterinarian, including: Changes in milk appearance (thicker, often yellowish to brown) Decreased milk production Decline in feed intake Fever Respiratory symptoms Changes in manure Steep drop in rumination and rumen motility If you notice any of these signs, isolate affected animals and contact your veterinarian and WSDA at 360-902-1878 or ahealth@agr.wa.gov. Most cattle affected by HPAI recover with supportive care with full herd recovery typically taking 4-6 weeks. “Seeing the virus move to another county is disappointing but our dairy farmers are working hard to implement their biosecurity plans, share lessons learned and help each other get through this,” said Washington State Veterinarian Amber Itle, VMD, MS. "This isn’t new for the country, but it is new for Washington. I’ve been in awe of how hard our veterinarians and dairy farmers work together every day to keep their cows healthy, keep their workers safe and keep operating despite all the uncertainty this virus brings with it. This detection was through routine surveillance enabling us to detect the virus before cows got sick. We hope this will help us to implement measures on farm to prevent transmission within or between other dairy or poultry facilities.” HPAI can spread between dairy cattle through infected animals and contaminated milk, equipment, vehicles, clothing, footwear and other materials or people that move between farms. Wild birds can also carry HPAI, but they are not considered the primary source of spread of the virus that affects dairy herds. Poultry are also highly susceptible to HPAI. Other states have reported infections in commercial and backyard poultry flocks near dairy farms affected by H5N1. Poultry owners, including those who keep backyard flocks, should remain vigilant for signs of illness and practice strong biosecurity to help reduce the risk of infection. (Continue . . .) According the WSDA, there are nearly 400 dairy farms in Washington State, which suggests that over the past 3 weeks roughly 7% of their dairy herds have tested positive for H5N1. Dairy product safety Pasteurization inactivates viruses and bacteria in milk, including HPAI virus, helping ensure the safety of the dairy supply. Infected cows can shed the virus in their milk, making raw milk and other raw dairy products unsafe for consumption. Avoid raw dairy product consumption, and do not allow your pets to consume raw milk or other dairy products, or raw foods such as raw meat. While the State of Washington posted the above warning on October 8th, Washington allows the sale of raw milk in grocery stores, natural food markets, food co-ops, and direct-to-consumer farm stores. Hopefully, the public is taking these risks seriously. ECDC & CDC Updates On Ebola Multi-country outbreak 2026 Credit CDC #19,388 With the number of confirmed cases nearing 10,000, the Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak in central Africa - which was first announced in mid-May in the DRC - is now the second largest in history, and shows no sign of stopping. Credit CDC This outbreak has spilled over into neighboring countries, and an imported case was recently reported in Nigeria (see ECDC Threat assessment brief – Importation of Ebola disease cases caused by Bundibugyo virus to Kenya and Nigeria). While sporadic exported cases are always possible, the public health risks outside of the DRC and surrounding areas is considered low. Yesterday the CDC (link) and the ECDC (link) both posted updated outbreak reports. Excerpts from both follow: Ebola disease: Multi-country outbreak 2026 This page is updated regularly. It was last updated on 26 October at 16:30. An outbreak of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus has been ongoing in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) since May 2026. Cases were also reported in Kenya and Nigeria in October 2026 and have been reported in Uganda, where the outbreak has ended. Key facts On 20 October 2026, an Ebola case was reported in Nigeria.
